title: Egg (oocyte) quality & oxidative stress
summary: Egg quality depends above all on age: chromosome errors driven by cohesin loss and declining mitochondrial function rise steeply after the mid-30s, and no lifestyle change or supplement has been shown to reverse that in humans. Within that limit, the biggest controllable factors are not smoking, avoiding obesity and heavy drinking, taking folic acid, and eating a Mediterranean-style diet in the ~3 months of follicle growth before conception or IVF. Antioxidant supplements, including CoQ10 and melatonin, have at best low-quality evidence for women, and ESHRE does not recommend antioxidant therapy in IVF.

factors.name: Female age (oocyte ageing)
factors.headline: Age is by far the dominant, non-modifiable driver of egg quality: fecundity falls from about 32 and faster after 37, and the share of women with no chromosomally normal embryo rises from 2-6% (age 26-37) to 33% at 42 and 53% at 44.

dose.effective: Not modifiable. The practical lever is time: ACOG/ASRM advise expedited evaluation after 6 months of trying from age 35, and immediate evaluation over 40.
dose.studied_range: Aneuploidy data from embryos of women aged ~22-47; egg chromosome-segregation data from ages 9-43.
dose.timeframe: Gradual decline from the early 30s, steep after ~37; no lifestyle change reverses it.
dose.notes: Lifestyle can avoid adding damage on top of age, but no diet or supplement has been shown to restore the chromosomal quality of older eggs in humans. Egg freezing at a younger age and IVF with PGT-A or donor eggs are the only interventions that address age directly.

factors.mechanism: Eggs are arrested in meiosis for decades. Cohesin that holds sister chromatids together is laid down before birth and is not renewed, so it erodes with age, causing chromosome mis-segregation (aneuploidy). In parallel, oocyte mitochondria become less efficient (less ATP, more mtDNA instability), CoQ10-synthesis enzymes and NAD+ levels decline (animal data), and spindle assembly becomes error-prone.
factors.interactions: Age magnifies almost every other harm: [egg-smoking] and [egg-obesity] effects are layered on a declining baseline. Diet associations such as [egg-mediterranean-diet] were seen only in women under 35 in one cohort. Supplements aimed at mitochondria ([egg-coq10], [egg-nmn-nad]) target the age mechanism but have no human live-birth proof.
factors.caveats: Aneuploidy also rises slightly in the very young (U-curve), but this is a minor effect compared with the rise after the mid-30s. Ovarian reserve tests (AMH, antral follicle count) predict egg number and response to stimulation, not egg quality; a woman with high AMH at 42 still has age-typical aneuploidy rates. Claims that any supplement 'reverses egg ageing' are not supported by human data.

factors.name: Polycystic ovary syndrome (PCOS)
factors.headline: PCOS carries measurable systemic oxidative stress (malondialdehyde about 47% higher, glutathione about 50% lower than controls, independent of weight); fertility problems are mainly ovulatory, and IVF outcomes are worse when PCOS coexists with obesity.

dose.effective: Management per the 2023 international guideline: healthy lifestyle first, then evidence-based medical and fertility treatment. In overweight women, losing 5% or more of body weight improved insulin, SHBG and cycles in an early study.
dose.studied_range: Weight loss studies 5-22% of body weight; lifestyle RCTs mostly 3-12 months.
dose.timeframe: Metabolic and ovulatory improvement over 3-6 months of weight loss.
dose.notes: Insulin resistance and hyperandrogenism, not oocytes per se, drive most of the problem; egg quality in lean, ovulating PCOS is often normal.

factors.mechanism: Hyperinsulinaemia and hyperandrogenism alter the follicular environment; chronic low-grade inflammation and lower antioxidant reserve (glutathione, paraoxonase-1) increase lipid peroxidation. Obesity adds lipotoxicity and further insulin resistance.
factors.interactions: Strongly interacts with [egg-obesity] and [egg-diabetes-insulin-resistance]; supplements studied mainly in PCOS: [egg-myo-inositol], [egg-nac]. Weight loss is covered by [egg-weight-loss].
factors.caveats: Raised oxidative markers in blood do not prove oxidative damage to eggs is the cause of infertility in PCOS; most infertility is anovulation, which is treatable. Lifestyle RCTs in PCOS have not reported live birth (Cochrane 2019 found none).

factors.name: Endometriosis
factors.headline: Endometriosis is an inflammatory, pro-oxidant condition linked to fewer and less mature eggs and lower oocyte mitochondrial content, but women with endometrioma have similar IVF live birth rates (OR 0.98) once eggs are retrieved.

dose.effective: Specialist management; surgery for endometrioma before IVF did not improve live birth (OR 0.90) and may reduce ovarian reserve.
dose.notes: Discuss fertility preservation and surgery timing with a reproductive specialist.

factors.mechanism: Peritoneal and follicular inflammation, iron from repeated bleeding (free-iron Fenton chemistry) and granulosa-cell ROS impair follicle development and oocyte maturation.
factors.interactions: Antioxidant supplements have been tried, but none has convincing live-birth data ([egg-antioxidant-supplements]).
factors.caveats: Evidence on egg quality is mostly from small biological studies; the main clinical effect is fewer oocytes and more cancelled cycles rather than lower live birth per transfer.

factors.name: Diabetes and insulin resistance
factors.headline: Women with type 1 or type 2 diabetes have 24-36% lower fecundability; in mice, maternal diabetes damages oocyte mitochondria and raises egg aneuploidy.

dose.effective: Good glycaemic control before conception (managed with the diabetes team); weight loss and physical activity for insulin resistance.
dose.timeframe: Preconception optimisation over at least 3 months covers one full cycle of follicle growth.
dose.notes: Preconception glucose control is also critical for reducing birth-defect risk.

factors.mechanism: Hyperglycaemia increases mitochondrial superoxide and advanced glycation end-products; in diabetic mice oocytes show abnormal mitochondrial structure, lower ATP and TCA metabolites, spindle defects and aneuploidy, and the defective mitochondria are passed to the embryo.
factors.interactions: Overlaps with [egg-obesity] and [egg-pcos].
factors.caveats: Oocyte mechanism data are from animals; human data are fecundability associations.

factors.name: Obesity (BMI 30 or higher)
factors.headline: Obesity (BMI >= 30) is associated with about 15% lower IVF live birth (RR 0.85), worse with PCOS, and with an inflamed, lipid-rich follicular environment.

dose.effective: Aim for BMI under 30 and ideally 18.5-24.9; in PCOS, even 5% weight loss improved hormones and cycles.
dose.studied_range: BMI categories 18.5-24.9 vs >= 30 kg/m2 in meta-analysis.
dose.too_much: Underweight (BMI < 18.5) and very low energy availability also impair ovulation (see [egg-vigorous-exercise-red-s]).
dose.timeframe: Follicular environment reflects the preceding ~3 months.
dose.notes: Donor-egg data did not change the overall conclusion, suggesting both egg and uterine effects.

factors.mechanism: Higher follicular fluid insulin, triglycerides, lactate and CRP; lipid accumulation in oocytes causes ER stress, reduced mitochondrial membrane potential and cumulus-cell apoptosis (lipotoxicity).
factors.interactions: Compounds [egg-pcos] and [egg-diabetes-insulin-resistance]. Weight-loss evidence is in [egg-weight-loss]. Vigorous exercise was not harmful in women with BMI >= 25 ([egg-moderate-exercise]).
factors.caveats: Associations are confounded by PCOS and metabolic disease. Weight-loss RCTs before IVF have not raised IVF live birth (see [egg-weight-loss]).

key_numbers.label: IVF live birth, BMI >= 30 vs normal

factors.name: Chemotherapy and pelvic radiation
factors.headline: Gonadotoxic chemotherapy and ovarian radiation destroy the egg reserve directly; less than 2 Gy is estimated to kill half of human oocytes.

dose.effective: Fertility-preservation counselling before treatment; egg or embryo freezing is standard care.
dose.too_much: Oocyte LD50 estimated at < 2 Gy; chemotherapy risk depends on drug (e.g. cyclophosphamide, doxorubicin), cumulative dose and age.
dose.timeframe: Primordial-follicle oocytes die within 12-24 h of gonadotoxic drug exposure, so preservation must happen before treatment.
dose.notes: GnRH agonists may be offered (e.g. breast cancer) but are not a substitute for proven preservation methods.

factors.mechanism: DNA double-strand breaks in primordial-follicle oocytes trigger apoptosis; radiation generates ROS and direct DNA damage.
factors.interactions: No antioxidant has been shown to protect human ovaries from chemotherapy.
factors.caveats: This is a medical-referral factor, not a lifestyle one.

factors.name: Cigarette smoking
factors.headline: Smoking is the largest avoidable toxic exposure for eggs: about 60% higher odds of infertility, roughly halved odds of IVF live birth (OR 0.54), lower AMH and twice the risk of early menopause.

dose.effective: Zero. Risk is dose-dependent (cigarettes/day, years smoked, pack-years).
dose.studied_range: Current vs never smokers; dose-response up to >20 cigarettes/day and 15-20+ years.
dose.too_much: Any active smoking. 11-15 pack-years: ~4-fold risk of premature menopause; 15-20 years' duration: much higher.
dose.timeframe: Quitting at least 3 months before trying covers one follicle-growth cycle; menopause-timing risk normalises about 10 years after quitting.
dose.notes: ASRM's 2024 opinion also reviews nicotine and marijuana as potential reproductive harms.

factors.mechanism: Tobacco smoke delivers polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons, cadmium and other oxidants that accelerate follicle loss (lower AMH), raise follicular oxidative stress and impair oocyte maturation.
factors.interactions: Adds to [egg-maternal-age]. Cadmium overlaps with [egg-heavy-metals]. Cessation is covered by [egg-smoking-cessation].
factors.caveats: Evidence is observational, but consistent across designs and dose-dependent, which supports causation.

key_numbers.label: IVF live birth per cycle, smokers

factors.name: Stopping smoking
factors.headline: Quitting removes the biggest avoidable egg toxin; former smokers' excess menopause risk is much smaller than current smokers' and disappears about 10 years after quitting.

dose.effective: Complete cessation, ideally at least 3 months before trying or before IVF stimulation.
dose.studied_range: Former vs current smokers, years since quitting.
dose.timeframe: One follicle-growth cycle (~3 months) for the follicular environment; longer for ovarian-reserve effects.
dose.notes: Lost follicles are not regained, so earlier is better. Use evidence-based cessation support.

factors.mechanism: Removes the exogenous oxidant and toxicant load (PAHs, cadmium) on growing follicles.
factors.interactions: See [egg-smoking].
factors.caveats: No RCT has randomised women to quit and measured egg quality; the benefit is inferred from the dose-response and former-smoker data.

factors.name: Alcohol
factors.headline: Heavier drinking lowers fertility, but under about 7 drinks a week effects on conception are small or undetectable; one IVF cohort saw 16% lower live birth at 4 or more drinks a week.

dose.effective: Ideally none while trying; if drinking, keep well under 4 drinks/week before and during IVF.
dose.studied_range: 0 to >= 14 servings/week; light <= 12.5 g ethanol/day vs >12.5 g/day.
dose.too_much: >= 4 drinks/week associated with lower IVF live birth (OR 0.84); >12.5 g/day (about one drink/day) with ~23% lower fecundability; ASRM: >2 drinks/day best avoided.
dose.timeframe: Preconception months; stop entirely once pregnancy is possible (fetal safety).
dose.notes: Data do not separate binge from regular drinking; binge drinking in the fertile window is probably worse.

factors.mechanism: Ethanol metabolism generates acetaldehyde and ROS (CYP2E1), disturbs estrogen and LH signalling, and depletes antioxidant reserves.
factors.interactions: Effects combine across partners in IVF (both drinking >= 4/week: OR 0.79).
factors.caveats: Studies conflict: a large Danish cohort found no effect below 14/week, and the EARTH IVF cohort found no effect of <= 12 g/day. The pregnancy-safety case for abstinence is stronger than the egg-quality case.

factors.name: Caffeine (high intake)
factors.headline: Moderate caffeine (under ~200 mg/day) shows little or no effect on conceiving or IVF success; the clearer risk is miscarriage once pregnant, rising about 7% per 100 mg/day.

dose.effective: Keep under 200 mg/day (about 1-2 cups of brewed coffee) while trying and in pregnancy.
dose.studied_range: <50 to >700 mg/day.
dose.too_much: > 500 mg/day linked to lower fertility (ASRM); in pregnancy, 350-699 mg/day RR 1.40 and >= 700 mg/day RR 1.72 for pregnancy loss.
dose.timeframe: Matters most from conception onward.
dose.notes: Keep fertility and miscarriage data separate: preconception intake was not associated with miscarriage in a large Danish cohort; early-pregnancy intake was.

factors.mechanism: Adenosine-receptor antagonism; effects on ovulation and tubal function are speculative. Not primarily an oxidative-stress factor.
factors.interactions: Coffee and tea are also polyphenol sources; there is no evidence that this offsets or adds to the caffeine effect on fertility. For general (non-pregnancy) oxidative-stress effects of coffee, see [coffee].
factors.caveats: Observational and confounded by pregnancy nausea (women with healthier pregnancies feel sick and drink less coffee). Male caffeine intake >= 300 mg/day was associated with lower fecundability in one cohort.

key_numbers.label: Miscarriage risk per +100 mg/day in pregnancy

factors.name: Air pollution (NO2, fine particles)
factors.headline: Higher traffic-related NO2 exposure is associated with lower AMH and lower IVF live birth (e.g. OR 0.76 per 0.01 ppm after embryo transfer); effect sizes per person are modest and hard to separate from other urban factors.

dose.effective: Reduce exposure where practical: avoid exercising beside heavy traffic, use HEPA filtration indoors on high-pollution days.
dose.studied_range: Residential and IVF-lab NO2, ozone, PM2.5 and PM10 from monitoring models.
dose.too_much: No safe threshold established; associations were per 0.01 ppm (Legro) or 20 ppb (Gaskins) increase in NO2.
dose.timeframe: Exposure in the ~3 months before IVF was studied.
dose.notes: In one IVF cohort the NO2-live birth association was absent in women taking >= 800 ug/day supplemental folate (hypothesis-generating).

factors.mechanism: Inhaled particles and NO2 cause systemic inflammation and oxidative stress; PAHs adsorbed on particles are ovotoxic.
factors.interactions: Possible modification by [egg-folic-acid]. Overlaps with [egg-smoking] (shared PAH exposure).
factors.caveats: All observational, with exposure estimated from home address. Individual control is limited; do not let this become a source of anxiety.

key_numbers.label: IVF live birth per +0.01 ppm NO2 (post-transfer)

factors.name: Phthalates (DEHP and related plasticizers)
factors.headline: In the EARTH IVF cohort, women in the top quartile of urinary DEHP metabolites had fewer eggs and about 19 percentage points lower live birth per cycle than the bottom quartile.

dose.effective: Lower exposure: eat more fresh, less ultra-processed and packaged food; avoid heating food in plastic; choose fragrance-free personal-care products.
dose.studied_range: Quartiles of urinary phthalate metabolites (spot urine samples).
dose.too_much: No established threshold; risk scaled with quartile.
dose.timeframe: Urinary levels vary day to day, reflecting recent exposure; follicles develop over ~3 months, so reduce exposure across that window.
dose.notes: Single EARTH cohort with 256 women; replication is limited.

factors.mechanism: Anti-androgenic and endocrine-disrupting effects on granulosa-cell steroidogenesis; animal studies show follicular oxidative stress and atresia.
factors.interactions: Often co-occurs with [egg-bpa] exposure from packaged food.
factors.caveats: Urine levels fluctuate day to day, so single samples misclassify exposure; confounding by diet quality is possible.

key_numbers.label: Live birth difference, top vs bottom DEHP quartile

factors.name: Bisphenol A (BPA)
factors.headline: Each log-unit increase in urinary BPA was associated with 12% fewer eggs retrieved in IVF; BPA causes egg aneuploidy in animals, but human outcome data are small and inconsistent.

dose.effective: Reduce exposure: fewer canned foods, avoid polycarbonate containers and heating food in plastic, minimise thermal-paper receipts.
dose.studied_range: Urinary BPA < 0.4 to 25.5 ug/L.
dose.timeframe: Reduce exposure across the ~3-month follicle-growth window.
dose.notes: Human data come from small IVF cohorts at one clinic.

factors.mechanism: Estrogen-receptor activity; in animals disrupts meiotic spindle formation and steroidogenesis and increases oxidative stress.
factors.interactions: [egg-phthalates] come from similar sources.
factors.caveats: Small cohorts (84 women); human evidence is not strong enough to quantify live-birth effects.

key_numbers.label: Oocytes retrieved per log-unit urinary BPA

factors.name: Heavy metals (mercury, lead, cadmium)
factors.headline: Higher follicular-fluid mercury (above ~0.5 ug/L) and lead were associated with lower IVF live birth (lead RR 0.68) in a small study; cadmium exposure comes mainly from smoking.

dose.effective: Favour smaller, lower-mercury fish over large predatory fish (e.g. shark, swordfish); do not smoke (main cadmium source).
dose.studied_range: Follicular fluid Hg, Pb, Cd, As in 56 IVF patients.
dose.too_much: Follicular fluid Hg > ~0.51 ug/L associated with lower biochemical pregnancy and live birth.
dose.notes: Keep eating fish: the omega-3 benefit is real; choose low-mercury species.

factors.mechanism: Metals bind thiol groups, deplete glutathione and inactivate antioxidant enzymes; cadmium and lead can displace essential metals and promote Fenton-type ROS generation.
factors.interactions: Trades off against [egg-omega-3] (fish is the main source of both); [egg-smoking] supplies cadmium.
factors.caveats: One small cohort; associations were non-linear and imprecise.

key_numbers.label: IVF live birth, higher follicular lead

factors.name: Very intense exercise and low energy availability (RED-S)
factors.headline: In lean women, 5 or more hours a week of vigorous exercise was associated with about 32% lower monthly chance of conception; exercising to exhaustion or on most days was linked to 2-3 times the odds of fertility problems.

dose.effective: If trying to conceive and lean, cap vigorous exercise below ~5 h/week and swap some for moderate activity; eat enough to keep regular cycles.
dose.studied_range: Vigorous activity 0 to >= 5 h/week (Danish cohort); frequency/intensity categories (Norwegian cohort).
dose.too_much: >= 5 h/week vigorous: FR 0.68 in lean women; exercising most days: 3.2-fold odds of fertility problems; exercising to exhaustion: 2.3-fold.
dose.timeframe: Cycle recovery after restoring energy balance can take months.
dose.notes: Missed or irregular periods in an active woman are a red flag for low energy availability (hypothalamic suppression).

factors.mechanism: Low energy availability suppresses GnRH pulsatility (functional hypothalamic amenorrhea), lowering estrogen and ovulation; this is an energy-signalling problem more than an oxidative one.
factors.interactions: No adverse association in women with BMI >= 25, for whom activity helps ([egg-moderate-exercise], [egg-weight-loss]). Different from acute oxidative damage after ultra-endurance events ([overtraining-ultraendurance]); in general health, vigorous exercise in normal amounts is beneficial ([hiit-vigorous-exercise]).
factors.caveats: Observational and self-reported; vigorous exercise was not associated with worse IVF outcomes in the EARTH cohort.

factors.name: Moderate physical activity
factors.headline: Moderate activity (e.g. brisk walking, cycling) is linked to slightly higher fecundability (FR 1.18 at >= 5 h/week) and, in women with reproductive problems, exercise interventions roughly doubled pregnancy rates in small trials.

dose.effective: Regular moderate activity; >= 5 h/week of moderate activity was associated with slightly higher fecundability, and any activity type helped women with BMI >= 25.
dose.studied_range: Moderate activity < 1 to >= 5 h/week; intervention trials mainly in PCOS and obesity.
dose.too_much: See [egg-vigorous-exercise-red-s]: >= 5 h/week vigorous activity in lean women.
dose.timeframe: Insulin sensitivity improves within weeks; ovulatory changes over months.
dose.notes: Pre-IVF activity (median 2.8 h/week moderate-to-vigorous) was not harmful.

factors.mechanism: Improves insulin sensitivity and reduces inflammation; regular moderate exercise up-regulates endogenous antioxidant defenses (hormesis).
factors.interactions: Combines with [egg-weight-loss] in overweight women.
factors.caveats: Intervention trials are few and small; the benefit is clearest in women with PCOS or overweight.

key_numbers.label: Pregnancy, PA intervention vs no therapy

factors.name: Poor sleep and circadian disruption
factors.headline: Frequent trouble sleeping was associated with about 13% lower monthly chance of conception; shift work is linked to menstrual disruption and night shifts to early miscarriage, but not clearly to infertility.

dose.effective: Aim for 7-9 h/night with a regular schedule; treat insomnia and sleep apnea.
dose.studied_range: Sleep < 6 to >= 9 h/day; shift vs day work.
dose.too_much: Trouble sleeping > 50% of nights: FR 0.87; night shifts: aOR 1.41 for early pregnancy loss.
dose.notes: Melatonin supplements are discussed separately ([egg-melatonin]); they are not a substitute for sleep.

factors.mechanism: Ovarian and pituitary clocks regulate the LH surge; circadian disruption alters melatonin (a follicular antioxidant), cortisol and insulin sensitivity.
factors.interactions: Overlaps with [egg-psychological-stress]. The shift-work findings also apply to [shift-work-circadian].
factors.caveats: Observational and confounded by depression and stress; shift work-infertility association lost significance after adjustment.

key_numbers.label: Fecundability, trouble sleeping > 50% of the time

factors.name: Psychological stress
factors.headline: A high salivary alpha-amylase stress marker was linked to 29% lower fecundability in one cohort, but a meta-analysis of 3583 IVF patients found pre-treatment anxiety or depression did not affect pregnancy rates.

dose.effective: Stress management for wellbeing (counselling, CBT, mindfulness, exercise); not proven to raise pregnancy rates.
dose.notes: Reassure people that stress caused by infertility does not ruin their IVF chances.

factors.mechanism: Sympathetic and HPA-axis activation can suppress GnRH/LH and raise systemic oxidative stress, but direct evidence of oocyte damage in humans is lacking.
factors.interactions: Linked with [egg-sleep-circadian].
factors.caveats: Reverse causation (infertility causes stress) is likely in many studies; avoid blaming patients.

factors.name: Mediterranean-style diet
factors.headline: Women in the lowest third of Mediterranean-diet adherence had much lower IVF live birth (26.6% vs 48.8%) in a Greek cohort of women under 35, but pooled evidence is inconsistent and no RCT has tested it.

dose.effective: Daily vegetables, fruit, legumes, whole grains, olive oil and nuts; fish 2+ times/week; little processed meat, sweets and refined snacks.
dose.studied_range: MedDietScore 0-55 (tertiles <= 30 vs >= 36); EARTH quartiles.
dose.timeframe: Adopt at least 3 months before trying or IVF.
dose.notes: In the US EARTH cohort, benefit plateaued after the second quartile: the gain comes from avoiding a poor diet rather than perfect adherence.

factors.mechanism: Supplies folate, vitamin B6, omega-3 and polyphenols, lowers homocysteine and systemic inflammation, and improves insulin sensitivity; higher blood and follicular-fluid folate/B6 were seen with this pattern.
factors.interactions: Overlaps with [egg-profertility-diet], [egg-folic-acid] and [egg-omega-3]; also supports [egg-weight-loss].
factors.caveats: All observational; association seen only in women under 35 in one study and no association with oocyte yield or embryo quality. A 2023 meta-analysis judged the evidence insufficient for clinical application.

key_numbers.label: IVF live birth, lowest vs highest tertile

factors.name: "Profertility" diet pattern (EARTH study)
factors.headline: A pattern of supplemental folic acid, B12 and vitamin D plus low-pesticide produce, whole grains, dairy, soy and seafood was associated with 53% higher odds of IVF live birth per SD of adherence (top vs bottom quartile: +28 percentage points).

dose.effective: Folic acid supplement (>= 400-800 ug/day), adequate B12 and vitamin D, whole grains, dairy, soy foods, seafood instead of other meats, and lower-pesticide-residue fruit and vegetables.
dose.studied_range: Quartiles of a score from a validated food-frequency questionnaire.
dose.timeframe: Diet in the year before treatment was measured.
dose.notes: Not related to estradiol, oocyte counts or endometrial thickness; associated with less clinical pregnancy loss.

factors.mechanism: Likely via one-carbon metabolism (folate/B12), vitamin D signalling and lower pesticide exposure rather than a direct antioxidant effect.
factors.interactions: Contains [egg-folic-acid] and [egg-vitamin-d]; overlaps with [egg-mediterranean-diet] and [egg-omega-3].
factors.caveats: Derived and tested in the same single US cohort (357 women) by the same group, which risks overfitting; needs independent replication or an RCT.

key_numbers.label: IVF live birth odds per SD adherence
Live birth, top vs bottom quartile

factors.name: Folic acid / folate
factors.headline: Folic acid is mandatory preconception care (400-800 ug/day prevents neural tube defects) and is also consistently associated with better fertility: 15% higher fecundability and 20 percentage points higher IVF live birth at > 800 ug/day supplemental folate.

dose.effective: 400-800 ug/day folic acid, started before conception (ideally 3 months ahead) and continued through early pregnancy.
dose.studied_range: Supplemental folate < 400 to > 800 ug/day (cohorts).
dose.too_much: Higher doses only on a clinician's advice for specific indications.
dose.timeframe: Before conception for neural tube protection; 3 months covers follicle development.
dose.notes: Usually taken as a prenatal multivitamin. Diet folate (leafy greens, legumes) is good but does not replace the supplement.

factors.mechanism: Folate supports one-carbon metabolism: DNA synthesis and repair, methylation and homocysteine clearance. Elevated homocysteine in follicular fluid is linked to poorer embryo quality.
factors.interactions: Core of [egg-profertility-diet]; may buffer the [egg-air-pollution] association in one cohort.
factors.caveats: Fertility benefits are observational; the neural-tube benefit is RCT-proven and reason enough to take it.

factors.name: Vitamin D (correcting deficiency)
factors.headline: Vitamin D-replete women had about 33% higher odds of IVF live birth than deficient women, but RCTs of supplementation in deficient women improved only chemical pregnancy, not clinical pregnancy.

dose.effective: Test 25(OH)D and correct deficiency with a clinician; there is no evidence that extra vitamin D helps women who are already replete.
dose.studied_range: Observational: replete vs deficient/insufficient 25(OH)D; 5 RCTs of supplementation in deficient women.
dose.too_much: Avoid unsupervised megadoses.
dose.timeframe: Correct deficiency before IVF or trying, within the 3-month preparation window.
dose.notes: Benefit, if any, is limited to correcting deficiency.

factors.mechanism: Vitamin D receptors are present in granulosa cells and endometrium; vitamin D influences AMH signalling and immune tolerance.
factors.interactions: Part of [egg-profertility-diet].
factors.caveats: Observational links are confounded by overall health, BMI and outdoor activity; RCT evidence is small.

key_numbers.label: IVF live birth, replete vs deficient

factors.name: Omega-3 fats (EPA/DHA from fish)
factors.headline: Each 1% higher serum long-chain omega-3 was associated with 8% higher probability of IVF live birth; in mice omega-3-rich diets preserved egg quality into older age.

dose.effective: Eat lower-mercury fatty fish regularly as part of the diet; studies measured serum levels and dietary share rather than a fixed supplement dose (replacing 1% of energy from saturated fat with long-chain omega-3 was associated with RR 2.37 for live birth).
dose.studied_range: Serum omega-3 4.7% median (IQR 3.8-5.8%) of total fatty acids.
dose.too_much: High-mercury fish (see [egg-heavy-metals]).
dose.timeframe: Adopt within the 3-month preconception window.
dose.notes: Human evidence is from observational IVF cohorts; no adequate RCT on live birth.

factors.mechanism: Incorporation into membranes, anti-inflammatory lipid mediators, possible effects on follicular steroidogenesis.
factors.interactions: Trade-off with [egg-heavy-metals]; part of [egg-mediterranean-diet] and [egg-profertility-diet].
factors.caveats: Small cohort (100 women); mouse data on reproductive ageing have not been replicated in humans.

key_numbers.label: IVF live birth probability per +1% serum LC omega-3

factors.name: Weight loss when overweight or obese
factors.headline: In overweight and obese women, diet-plus-exercise programmes increased natural pregnancy (RR 1.59) and ovulation, but two RCTs (LIFEstyle, Nordic trial) found that delaying fertility treatment for weight loss did not improve live birth from treatment.

dose.effective: 5-10% of body weight via a reduced-calorie diet plus aerobic exercise; >5% loss improved insulin and cycles in PCOS.
dose.studied_range: Mean losses 4.4 kg (LIFEstyle, 6 months) to 9.4 kg (12 weeks of 880 kcal/day low-calorie diet).
dose.too_much: Do not delay treatment for long in women over ~35: time lost costs egg quality ([egg-maternal-age]).
dose.timeframe: 3-6 months.
dose.notes: Weight loss increased spontaneous conceptions (10.5% vs 2.6% in the Nordic trial). Best for women not yet in IVF or with anovulation.

factors.mechanism: Lowers insulin and free androgens, raises SHBG, reduces follicular lipid and inflammatory load (lipotoxicity).
factors.interactions: Works with [egg-moderate-exercise] and [egg-mediterranean-diet]; counteracts [egg-obesity] and [egg-pcos].
factors.caveats: LIFEstyle: 27.1% vs 35.2% healthy term singleton births, favouring prompt treatment, partly because the intervention arm delayed treatment by 6 months. Weight loss is still worthwhile for pregnancy health.

factors.name: Antioxidant supplements in general (for the female partner)
factors.headline: The Cochrane review of 63 trials found only low- to very-low-quality evidence that antioxidants help subfertile women, several included trials have since been retracted, and ESHRE does not recommend antioxidant therapy in IVF.

dose.effective: No antioxidant product or dose is proven to raise live birth in women.
dose.studied_range: Trials of NAC, melatonin, L-arginine, myo-inositol, carnitine, selenium, vitamins C/E/D, B complex, CoQ10 and omega-3, usually for 1-3 cycles.
dose.too_much: No clear harms in pooled data (miscarriage OR 1.13, GI effects OR 1.55, both NS), but in animals blocking ROS impairs ovulation, so more is not better.
dose.timeframe: Trials typically 1-3 months.
dose.notes: Cochrane's headline OR for live birth (1.81) rests on very-low-quality, small, often unregistered trials; treat it as unreliable. A 2026 editorial note lists 7 retracted and 2 'concern' trials in the review.

factors.mechanism: Direct scavengers cannot reach the mitochondrial sites where oocyte ROS are generated at meaningful concentrations, and ROS are required for LH-triggered ovulation; the 'antioxidant paradox' applies.
factors.interactions: Specific agents are listed separately: [egg-coq10], [egg-melatonin], [egg-myo-inositol], [egg-nac], [egg-vitamin-e-c], [egg-l-carnitine], [egg-alpha-lipoic-acid], [egg-resveratrol], [egg-nmn-nad]. Antioxidants for the male partner are a different question.
factors.caveats: Supplement marketing for 'egg quality' far outruns the evidence. Spending on lifestyle basics and folic acid is better supported.

key_numbers.label: Live birth, antioxidants vs control (very low quality)

factors.name: Coenzyme Q10 (ubiquinone/ubiquinol)
factors.headline: The best-studied 'egg quality' supplement: 600 mg/day for 60 days before IVF increased eggs retrieved (median 4 vs 2) and good embryos in young poor responders, and meta-analyses show higher clinical pregnancy (OR ~2.2-2.4) but no significant live-birth gain.

dose.effective: 600 mg/day (200 mg three times daily) for 60 days before IVF (Xu 2018 RCT).
dose.studied_range: 600 mg/day in the Xu RCT; pooled RCTs (5 trials, 449 women) used varying regimens.
dose.too_much: No harms reported in these trials.
dose.timeframe: At least 2 months before stimulation; ideally covering the ~3-month follicle-growth window.
dose.notes: Fat-soluble. Evidence is mainly in poor responders/low ovarian reserve; no good data in women with normal reserve.

factors.mechanism: CoQ10 carries electrons in the mitochondrial respiratory chain and is a lipid-phase antioxidant. Ageing oocytes in mice and women express less of the CoQ-synthesis enzymes PDSS2 and COQ6; in mice CoQ10 restored oocyte mitochondrial function and reduced spindle defects.
factors.interactions: Mechanistically overlaps with [egg-nmn-nad] (both target mitochondrial ageing). Often bundled with [egg-melatonin] and [egg-myo-inositol] in commercial products, which prevents attributing effects.
factors.caveats: Small trials; the Xu RCT was open-label without placebo and excluded 17 non-compliant women. ESHRE does not recommend antioxidant therapy in IVF. Not shown to reduce aneuploidy in humans.

key_numbers.label: Cumulative live birth, CoQ10 vs control (NS)

factors.name: Melatonin
factors.headline: Melatonin is a natural follicular antioxidant; in IVF RCTs it raised clinical pregnancy (OR 1.43) and egg/embryo counts in pooled low-quality data, but not live birth (OR 1.38, NS), and a placebo-controlled dose trial saw no change in follicle numbers.

dose.effective: 3 mg/day at night during IVF stimulation was the dose used in the early Japanese studies; not proven.
dose.studied_range: 3 mg/day to 8 mg twice daily.
dose.too_much: Higher doses (up to 8 mg twice daily) did not add benefit; doses below and above showed no live-birth difference in Cochrane comparisons.
dose.timeframe: Usually from early follicular phase to egg retrieval.
dose.notes: Melatonin is a hormone with circadian effects; doses up to 8 mg twice daily did not cause daytime sleepiness in an IVF trial, but there is no reason to use high doses.

factors.mechanism: Concentrated in follicular fluid, scavenges hydroxyl radicals and stimulates antioxidant enzymes; follicular melatonin was inversely related to 8-OHdG oxidative DNA damage.
factors.interactions: Frequently combined with [egg-myo-inositol]; a large combination trial was retracted in 2026.
factors.caveats: Trials are heterogeneous (PCOS to poor responders), small and low quality; the key Tamura data were non-randomized.

factors.name: Myo-inositol (in PCOS)
factors.headline: Widely used in PCOS, but the Cochrane review rated the evidence very low quality and could not show a live-birth benefit (OR 2.42, 95% CI 0.75-7.83); the 2023 PCOS guideline review calls it limited and inconclusive.

dose.effective: Trials commonly used 4 g/day myo-inositol with 400 ug folic acid (e.g. the now-retracted Pacchiarotti trial); no dose is proven to raise live birth.
dose.studied_range: 11 of 13 Cochrane trials used myo-inositol as pre-treatment before IVF; 2 during ovulation induction.
dose.too_much: Mild GI effects; fewer GI effects than metformin.
dose.timeframe: Pre-treatment before IVF stimulation in most trials.
dose.notes: D-chiro-inositol may help ovulation per the guideline review, but evidence is very uncertain. One widely cited myo-inositol plus melatonin RCT (526 women) was retracted in 2026.

factors.mechanism: Inositol phosphoglycans act as second messengers for insulin and FSH signalling; may improve insulin sensitivity in PCOS.
factors.interactions: Alternative to or adjunct with metformin; often combined with [egg-melatonin] and [egg-folic-acid].
factors.caveats: Industry-linked trials, poor reporting and a retraction. Not relevant for women without PCOS.

key_numbers.label: Live birth, MI vs standard (2 RCTs)

factors.name: N-acetylcysteine (NAC) in PCOS
factors.headline: In PCOS, NAC added to clomiphene improved ovulation and pregnancy vs placebo in small, biased trials, but it was inferior to metformin and live-birth data are thin.

dose.effective: 1.2 g/day (with clomiphene in clomiphene-resistant PCOS) in the original RCT.
dose.studied_range: 1.2 g/day in the main RCT; 8 RCTs (910 women) pooled in meta-analysis.
dose.timeframe: During ovulation-induction cycles.
dose.notes: A glutathione precursor; available as a supplement in some countries and a drug in others.

factors.mechanism: Supplies cysteine for glutathione synthesis; may improve insulin sensitivity.
factors.interactions: Compared against metformin and [egg-l-carnitine] in trials; the NAC-vs-carnitine trial in the Cochrane review was flagged for integrity concerns.
factors.caveats: Many trials come from a few centres; high risk of selection, attrition and reporting bias. The 1.2 g/day trial's 49% vs 1% ovulation contrast is implausibly large.

key_numbers.label: Ovulation, NAC + clomiphene vs placebo + clomiphene

factors.name: DHEA in poor responders
factors.headline: Cochrane (2024, moderate certainty): DHEA probably makes little or no difference to live birth in poor responders (OR 1.30, NS); testosterone pre-treatment looks more promising (OR 2.53). ESHRE does not recommend DHEA.

dose.effective: Not recommended. A typical trial dose was 75 mg/day before and during the IVF cycle.
dose.studied_range: 75 mg/day (Wiser 2010) and similar regimens.
dose.too_much: Androgenic side effects (acne, hair growth); a hormone, use only under medical supervision.
dose.timeframe: Started before the IVF cycle and continued during stimulation in trials.
dose.notes: Network meta-analysis showed higher clinical pregnancy with DHEA (OR 2.46), but the larger Cochrane pooled analysis with live birth as outcome did not.

factors.mechanism: Androgen precursor proposed to increase FSH sensitivity of small antral follicles; not an antioxidant.
factors.interactions: Compare [egg-coq10] in the same poor-responder population.
factors.caveats: Early small trials (e.g. 33 women) overstated benefit.

factors.name: Vitamin E and vitamin C supplements
factors.headline: Vitamin E (600 mg/day) lowered follicular oxidative markers in a tiny study, and supplement use was associated with slightly shorter time to pregnancy in some subgroups, but there is no convincing RCT evidence of more live births.

dose.effective: Meet needs from food (nuts, seeds, vegetable oils, fruit, vegetables); routine high-dose supplements are not supported.
dose.studied_range: Vitamin E 600 mg/day (Tamura); vitamin C and E in mixed antioxidant trials in the Cochrane review.
dose.too_much: No benefit shown, so there is no reason to take high-dose supplements.
dose.notes: Typical prenatal vitamins already contain modest amounts.

factors.mechanism: Vitamin E is the main lipid-phase chain-breaking antioxidant; vitamin C regenerates it. Neither targets mitochondrial ROS production.
factors.interactions: Part of [egg-antioxidant-supplements].
factors.caveats: Classic antioxidant paradox: big mechanistic story, no clinical proof.

factors.name: L-carnitine / acetyl-L-carnitine
factors.headline: Evidence for women is weak; the most-cited positive RCT (L-carnitine 3 g/day in clomiphene-resistant PCOS) has been retracted.

dose.effective: No proven dose for female fertility.
dose.studied_range: 3 g/day in the retracted PCOS trial.
dose.notes: Male-factor evidence is separate and somewhat better.

factors.mechanism: Shuttles long-chain fatty acids into mitochondria for beta-oxidation, which oocytes use for energy.
factors.interactions: Included in [egg-antioxidant-supplements] analyses.
factors.caveats: Retraction of the main trial removes the main human evidence.

factors.name: Resveratrol
factors.headline: Resveratrol may improve some follicular markers (an 800 mg/day RCT in PCOS raised oocyte maturity without changing pregnancy rates), but it suppresses endometrial decidualization, and 200 mg/day during embryo-transfer cycles was associated with lower pregnancy (OR 0.54) and more miscarriage (OR 2.60).

dose.effective: Not recommended while trying to conceive or around embryo transfer.
dose.studied_range: 200 mg/day (retrospective IVF cohort); 800 mg/day for 60 days (PCOS RCT, 56 women).
dose.too_much: Any use in the luteal phase or early pregnancy (possible anti-implantation effect; teratogenicity not excluded).
dose.notes: A clear example where an 'anti-ageing' antioxidant may harm the uterus even if it helps the ovary.

factors.mechanism: SIRT1 activation and antioxidant effects in the ovary; in endometrium it down-regulates the CRABP2-RAR pathway, inhibiting decidualization needed for implantation.
factors.interactions: Sirtuin-pathway overlap with [egg-nmn-nad].
factors.caveats: Harm signal is retrospective; benefit signal is a single small RCT on surrogate outcomes.

key_numbers.label: Clinical pregnancy, resveratrol during transfer cycles

factors.name: NMN / NAD+ precursors (NMN, NR)
factors.headline: NAD+ falls in ageing mouse eggs and NMN restored egg quality and fertility in aged mice, but there are no human data on egg quality, pregnancy or live birth.

dose.effective: No human fertility dose exists; all egg data are from mice.
dose.studied_range: Animal studies only.
dose.too_much: Unknown in pregnancy; safety in early embryos not studied in humans.
dose.notes: Marketed heavily as 'egg rejuvenation'; this is extrapolation from mice.

factors.mechanism: Raises NAD+, a cofactor for sirtuins (e.g. SIRT2) and mitochondrial metabolism; in aged mice restored spindle assembly, mitochondrial function and lowered ROS.
factors.interactions: Shares the mitochondrial-ageing target with [egg-coq10]; sirtuin overlap with [egg-resveratrol].
factors.caveats: Mouse reproductive ageing differs from human (human egg aneuploidy is driven largely by cohesin loss over decades).

factors.name: Alpha-lipoic acid (ALA)
factors.headline: A systematic review reports some positive effects on oocyte maturation, embryo grade and endometriosis pain, but the trials are small and no live-birth benefit has been shown.

dose.effective: No proven dose for female fertility.
dose.studied_range: Small trials, often combined with inositol or other agents.
dose.notes: Mostly from Italian combination-product studies.

factors.mechanism: Mitochondrial enzyme cofactor and redox-cycling antioxidant that regenerates glutathione, vitamins C and E.
factors.interactions: Usually given with [egg-myo-inositol].
factors.caveats: Evidence base is too weak to recommend.

factors.name: Curcumin supplements for PCOS and egg quality
factors.headline: In PCOS, several small RCTs and meta-analyses show curcumin modestly lowers fasting glucose (~3-4 mg/dL), insulin and HOMA-IR, without consistent effects on lipids, testosterone, LH/FSH or weight, and no trial has measured ovulation, pregnancy or live birth.

dose.effective: PCOS trials: 500-1500 mg/day standard curcumin or ~80 mg two to three times daily as nanocurcumin, for 8-12 weeks.
dose.studied_range: 80-240 mg/day nanocurcumin to 1500 mg/day standard curcumin; endometriosis-ART trial 120 mg/day nanomicelle for 10 weeks.
dose.too_much: Not established. EFSA ADI (3 mg/kg/day) rests on a multigeneration reproductive-toxicity study (reduced F2 body-weight gain). Mouse oocytes exposed to curcumin showed impaired maturation and embryo development. No human safety data in pregnancy at supplement doses.
dose.timeframe: Metabolic effects at 8-12 weeks; an oocyte matures over ~3 months.
dose.notes: Glycaemic benefit is small compared with metformin; one 200-woman factorial trial found curcumin plus metformin better than either alone. Stopping high-dose supplements once pregnancy is possible is a precautionary inference, not a tested rule.

factors.mechanism: Improved insulin sensitivity and lower inflammation/oxidative stress would plausibly help the ovarian environment in PCOS; animal studies show curcumin can preserve follicle reserve but other animal studies show direct harm to oocytes and embryos, so the net effect on eggs is unknown.
factors.interactions: Additive to metformin in one trial. Alternative or adjunct to [myo-inositol], which has a larger PCOS evidence base; no head-to-head trials. Treat [pcos] and [glycemic-control] first with lifestyle and established drugs. Same liver and drug-interaction cautions as [curcumin-supplements].
factors.caveats: All PCOS and endometriosis trials found here were small and mostly from Iran; meta-analyses pool 3-8 trials with high heterogeneity for HOMA-IR. A small endometriosis-ART trial reported more mature oocytes and good embryos but needs replication; a separate endometriosis RCT found no pain benefit. Oocyte-quality claims rest on conflicting animal data (mechanistic).

key_numbers.label: Fasting glucose change in PCOS (5 RCTs)

factors.name: Sulforaphane / broccoli sprouts for egg and ovarian function
factors.headline: No human trial has tested sulforaphane on egg quality, ovarian reserve, PCOS or IVF outcomes; it protects human granulosa cells and animal oocytes from oxidative stress in the lab, but becomes cytotoxic to granulosa cells at higher concentrations.

dose.effective: Unknown for ovarian outcomes; only general-health doses have been tested in people.
dose.studied_range: In vitro: about 1-5 µM in oocyte maturation or granulosa-cell culture.
dose.too_much: Bovine granulosa cells lost viability above about 15 µM in culture.
dose.timeframe: Follicle development takes about 3 months, so any dietary effect would need at least that long.
dose.notes: In vitro maturation results apply to IVF lab media, not diet.

factors.mechanism: Nrf2 activation (SOD, catalase, GCLC/GCLM, HO-1, NQO1) and AMPK/AKT signalling in granulosa cells and oocytes; reduced ROS, mitochondrial dysfunction and spindle defects after toxin exposure.
factors.interactions: Same redundancy considerations as [broccoli-sprouts] and [sulforaphane-supplements]. The modest glucose-lowering seen in obese people with poorly controlled diabetes ([glycemic-control]) is the only human finding with plausible indirect relevance to PCOS, and it has not been tested in PCOS.
factors.caveats: Cell and animal data only; biphasic (protective at low, harmful at high concentrations) responses argue against high-dose supplementation around conception without data.

factors.name: Astaxanthin before IVF/ICSI
factors.headline: Three small RCTs (PCOS, poor responders, endometriosis; 6-12 mg/day for 6-12 weeks) reported more mature (MII) oocytes and high-quality embryos, but the PCOS trial found no difference in pregnancy rates and none reported live births.

dose.effective: 6-12 mg/day for 40 days to 12 weeks before ovarian stimulation.
dose.studied_range: 6-12 mg/day, 40 days to 12 weeks.
dose.too_much: No safety signal in these short trials.
dose.timeframe: 6-12 weeks before stimulation.

factors.mechanism: Raised serum antioxidant capacity and granulosa-cell Nrf2/HO-1/NQO1 expression, and lowered follicular-fluid IL-6, IL-8 and cell-free DNA.
factors.interactions: Compare [egg-antioxidant-supplements], [egg-coq10] and [astaxanthin-supplement].
factors.caveats: Oocyte and embryo grades are surrogates; the trials are small; no live-birth data; independent replication is needed.

factors.name: Soy isoflavones and IVF outcomes
factors.headline: In a fertility-clinic cohort of 315 women (520 ART cycles), higher dietary soy isoflavone intake was associated with higher live-birth rates (adjusted OR about 1.8); no trial has tested it.

dose.effective: Habitual intakes of 2.6-28 mg/day isoflavones were in the higher-benefit categories.
dose.studied_range: 0-28 mg/day dietary isoflavones (observational).
dose.notes: Equol-producer status was not assessed.

factors.mechanism: Weak estrogen-receptor activity of isoflavones and equol has been proposed to aid endometrial receptivity; unproven.
factors.interactions: See [soy-isoflavones] and [egg-mediterranean-diet].
factors.caveats: Single observational cohort; residual confounding by diet pattern is likely.

key_numbers.label: Adjusted odds ratio of live birth, 2.6-7.6 mg/day vs none

factors.name: Spermidine for oocyte quality
factors.headline: Spermidine supplementation restored oocyte quality and fertility in aged mice by enhancing mitophagy, but there are no human data.

dose.effective: Not established.
dose.studied_range: Mouse and pig-oocyte studies only.

factors.mechanism: Ovarian spermidine falls with age in mice; supplementation improved mitophagy and mitochondrial function in oocytes.
factors.interactions: See [spermidine] for general human evidence.
factors.caveats: Animal-only; supplements marketed for egg quality are ahead of the data.

factors.name: Ketogenic / low-carbohydrate diet (PCOS and conception)
factors.headline: In overweight women with PCOS, ketogenic and low-carb diets cut weight (~5 kg more than other diets), LH and insulin resistance and appear to improve cycles and ovulation. In mice, though, ketone levels typical of keto slow embryo development and a gestational keto diet harms offspring, so the case for staying ketotic while trying to conceive is weak.

dose.effective: For overweight PCOS: 8-12 weeks of a ketogenic diet (< 20-50 g/day carbohydrate, often Mediterranean-style) or a moderate low-carbohydrate diet (< 45% of energy) aimed at weight loss. Then move to a sustainable lower-glycaemic diet with folate-rich foods plus a folic-acid supplement before trying to conceive.
dose.studied_range: PCOS trials: 45 days to 24 weeks, ketogenic (< 20-50 g/day) and very-low-energy ketogenic protocols; low-carb RCTs < 45% energy for > 4 weeks.
dose.too_much: Not recommended once trying to conceive or in pregnancy outside specialist care (epilepsy). Avoid in lean PCOS without weight to lose. Restricted carbohydrate intake was linked to half the dietary folic acid and 30% higher odds of neural tube defects.
dose.timeframe: Hormonal and menstrual changes over 8-24 weeks, alongside weight loss.
dose.notes: Grade honestly: most PCOS data are uncontrolled before-after studies or small RCTs. Pregnancy and live-birth data are anecdotal (2 conceptions in an 11-woman pilot). Benefits are hard to separate from weight loss.

factors.mechanism: Lower insulin reduces ovarian theca androgen production and raises SHBG. Weight loss lowers adipose inflammation and lipotoxicity. In PCOS mice, BHB reduced granulosa-cell inflammation and apoptosis. Against that, BHB at ~2 mmol/L (keto-diet levels) disturbed embryo glycolysis and histone acetylation and reduced viability in mouse embryo culture. A maternal keto diet raised BHB in oviduct fluid and delayed blastocyst development.
factors.interactions: Works through [egg-weight-loss] and [egg-diabetes-insulin-resistance]; see [egg-pcos] / [pcos]. Can be combined with [egg-myo-inositol]. Folate intake drops when grains are cut, so pair with [egg-folic-acid]. General-health effects are under [ketogenic-diet] and [low-carb-diet].
factors.caveats: Meta-analyses (2019-2026) agree on weight, insulin and LH but are inconsistent on androgens and lipids, with high heterogeneity. Two RCTs found no weight advantage over a matched low-calorie diet. Low-carb diets help reproductive outcomes in pooled PCOS RCTs, but the evidence is mostly not specific to ketosis. There are no human oocyte-quality data. The cautionary data (embryo, gestation, offspring lifespan) are mouse studies at diets more extreme than human keto, and the neural-tube association is observational.

key_numbers.label: Weight change vs other diets in PCOS
Ovulatory infertility RR, highest vs lowest carb intake

factors.name: Fasting, ovulation, PCOS and pregnancy
factors.headline: In PCOS, intermittent fasting lowered weight (-4.25 kg) and free androgen index and raised SHBG, but no more than calorie restriction; in lean women a 72-h fast made 2 of 7 cycles anovulatory, and fasting beyond the overnight period in late pregnancy rapidly produces ketosis.

dose.effective: With PCOS and excess weight: an 8-10 h eating window or daily calorie restriction for 8+ weeks, whichever is easier to keep. Without excess weight: avoid deliberate energy deficit while trying to conceive.
dose.studied_range: 72-h follicular-phase fasts; 5-12 weeks of 6-10 h TRE in PCOS; Ramadan in pregnancy.
dose.too_much: Energy availability below ~30 kcal/kg lean mass/day disrupts LH pulses; multi-day fasts in lean women can block ovulation. In pregnancy avoid fasting beyond the overnight period (18-h fasts cause ketonaemia).
dose.timeframe: Androgen and menstrual changes in PCOS over 5-8 weeks; follicle effects within one cycle.
dose.notes: Normal-weight women tolerated a 3-day fast without cycle disruption; lean women (<=20% body fat) did not.

factors.mechanism: In insulin-resistant PCOS, lower insulin raises SHBG and lowers ovarian androgen output. In lean women, energy deficit slows GnRH/LH pulsatility (hypothalamic suppression). In pregnancy, 'accelerated starvation' raises maternal ketones that cross the placenta.
factors.interactions: Works through the same route as [egg-weight-loss] in [pcos]. Stacking fasting with heavy training risks [vigorous-exercise-low-energy]. Prenatal nutrient needs (e.g., [egg-folic-acid]) are harder to meet in short eating windows.
factors.caveats: PCOS evidence is five small studies; the only RCT comparing early TRE with calorie restriction (Talebi 2024) found no difference. Ramadan pregnancy meta-analyses show no birth-weight effect but are observational and lack mortality data; the IQ-ketone link (Rizzo 1991) is correlational.

key_numbers.label: Weight change with IF in PCOS (meta-analysis)
Energy availability threshold for LH disruption
PCOS women with improved menstrual regularity after 5 weeks of 8-h TRE

factors.name: PFAS and female fertility
factors.headline: A Singapore preconception cohort found 5-10% lower fecundability per quartile of some PFAS and Chinese clinic studies link PFAS to PCOS and poorer embryo quality, but older time-to-pregnancy links were likely reverse causation, and PFAS did not track AMH or follicle counts.

dose.effective: No fertility intervention tested. For likely-exposed women, see [pfas] (testing, water filtration). Plasma donation and bile-acid sequestrants lower serum PFAS but have not been studied for fertility and sequestrants are not tested in pregnancy planning.
dose.studied_range: Plasma PFOS ~4-13 ng/mL in fertility cohorts; follicular fluid PFOA ~5-7 ng/mL.
dose.too_much: NASEM serum sum >20 ng/mL = increased general health risk.
dose.timeframe: Years (PFAS half-lives 2.7-5.3 years).
dose.notes: PFAS cross readily into follicular fluid (65-92% of serum levels). Pregnancy and breastfeeding lower a woman's PFAS, which is why parity confounds time-to-pregnancy studies.

factors.mechanism: PFAS in follicular fluid may disrupt steroidogenesis, PPAR signalling and follicular lipid metabolism; one IVF study linked PFOA to altered follicular sphingolipids and organonitrogen metabolites.
factors.interactions: Coexists with other persistent pollutants; in one ovarian-tissue study organochlorines, not PFAS, tracked a smaller ovarian reserve. Women's PFAS falls with each pregnancy and breastfeeding period.
factors.caveats: Mostly case-control or single-centre clinic studies; PCOS itself alters menstruation and therefore PFAS excretion (reverse causation).
factors.debate: Time to pregnancy: the Danish birth cohort found longer TTP with PFOS/PFOA [env-fei2009], but the link appeared only in parous women in Norway [env-whitworth2012], the original authors raised reverse causation [env-fei2012], and a systematic review judged it most likely not causal [env-bach2016]. A preconception cohort that avoids this bias still found modestly lower fecundability [env-cohen2023]. PCOS: a mixture of PFAS, led by newer alternatives, was associated with PCOS [env-zhan2023], whereas an earlier study found only one congener associated [env-wangw2019]. IVF: follicular PFOA tracked poorer embryo quality [env-xu2025], but another IVF study found no clear outcome pattern [env-hong2022]; PFAS were not associated with AMH or follicle density in ovarian tissue [env-bjorvang2021].

key_numbers.label: Subfecundity OR, top PFOS quartile, nulliparous women
PCOS odds per ln-unit PFAS mixture

factors.name: GLP-1 drugs before conception (PCOS, contraception, washout)
factors.headline: In PCOS with obesity GLP-1 drugs add modest weight loss (BMI -1.4 kg/m2 in 11 RCTs) but a fertility benefit is unproven; tirzepatide cut oral-contraceptive peak levels by 59%, and the semaglutide label says stop at least 2 months before trying to conceive.

dose.effective: Semaglutide or liraglutide in PCOS trials, usually 12-26 weeks before ovulation induction or IVF, followed by a drug-free gap.
dose.studied_range: Liraglutide 1.2 mg/day with metformin for 12 weeks then a 4-week washout before IVF (pilot RCT); 11 RCTs of GLP-1 add-on in PCOS.
dose.too_much: Continuing into pregnancy: the labels warn of possible fetal harm (from animal data) and human data on continued use are limited. Oral contraceptives may fail during tirzepatide start-up and dose escalation.
dose.timeframe: Semaglutide: discontinue >=2 months before a planned pregnancy (label). Tirzepatide: use non-oral or back-up contraception for 4 weeks after starting and after each dose increase (label).
dose.notes: Informs, does not prescribe: do not stop, start or change the dose of a prescribed medication without talking to the prescriber. Plan the washout and contraception with the prescriber; weight loss itself can restore ovulation, so unplanned pregnancies occur. Stop the drug and inform the prescriber if pregnancy is found.

factors.mechanism: Weight loss and lower insulin reduce ovarian androgen excess and can restore ovulation; GLP-1 receptors are also present in reproductive tissues. Delayed gastric emptying lowers and delays absorption of oral contraceptive hormones, most with tirzepatide after the first doses [med-fda-zepbound2023, med-skelley2024].
factors.interactions: An option alongside [metformin] and lifestyle in [pcos] and [excess-adiposity]; produces [weight-loss]. St John's wort is another cause of oral-contraceptive failure ([supplement-drug-interactions]). Folic acid ([folic-acid]) should start before the washout ends.
factors.caveats: Fertility trials are small, short and mostly use liraglutide; there are no large trials of semaglutide or tirzepatide with live birth as the outcome.
factors.debate: Benefit: a pilot RCT found higher IVF pregnancy rates with liraglutide plus metformin than metformin alone despite similar weight loss [med-salamun2018], and GLP-1 agonists beat metformin for weight and insulin sensitivity in PCOS [med-han2019]; but the 2026 guideline-informing meta-analysis found only modest weight loss and insufficient evidence for reproductive outcomes [med-forslund2026]. Safety: large cohorts found no excess malformations versus insulin [med-cesta2024] and no consistent safety signal [med-ozbek2026], with preterm-birth signals confined to women with diabetes [med-hviid2026]; an AJOG review argues malformation data cannot be trusted without glycaemic-control data and recommends contraception for all users [med-drummond2025].

key_numbers.label: BMI change, GLP-1 add-on in PCOS
Ethinyl estradiol Cmax fall after tirzepatide 5 mg

factors.name: NSAIDs around ovulation and conception
factors.headline: Continuous NSAIDs around ovulation caused luteinized unruptured follicles (the egg is not released) in 35.6% of cycles vs 3.4% untreated in women with arthritis, mostly with the COX-2 drug etoricoxib, while ibuprofen 1600 mg/day caused none; NSAIDs around conception were also linked to miscarriage (aHR 1.89).

dose.effective: Occasional NSAID doses for period pain are not implicated; concern is continuous use spanning ovulation.
dose.studied_range: Continuous periovulatory etoricoxib, diclofenac and ibuprofen 1600 mg/day (arthritis cohort); any NSAID use around conception (miscarriage cohort).
dose.too_much: Continuous periovulatory COX-2 inhibitor use; use for >=15 days around conception (aHR 1.85 for miscarriage).
dose.timeframe: Ovulation returns in the next cycle after stopping.
dose.notes: Informs, does not prescribe: do not stop, start or change the dose of a prescribed medication without talking to the prescriber. Women with inflammatory conditions planning pregnancy can discuss avoiding continuous NSAIDs around mid-cycle with their rheumatologist.

factors.mechanism: COX-2-derived prostaglandins drive the enzymatic breakdown of the follicle wall at ovulation; blocking them lets the follicle luteinize without releasing the egg [med-stone2002, med-micu2011].
factors.interactions: [acetaminophen] is the usual alternative around conception; relevant to [endometriosis] and inflammatory arthritis, where NSAIDs are common.
factors.caveats: Ovulation data come from women with inflammatory arthritis and small case series; the miscarriage link is observational and confounded by the reasons for taking NSAIDs.
factors.debate: Ovulation: case series and a monitored-cycle cohort show reversible ovulatory failure [med-smith1996, med-micu2011, med-stone2002], but evidence is limited to small samples. Pregnancy: a prospective cohort linked periconceptional NSAIDs to miscarriage, even versus acetaminophen users [med-li2018], while a 2024 meta-analysis found the miscarriage association non-significant (OR 1.20) but birth defects modestly higher (OR 1.19) [med-chen2024].

factors.name: Antidepressants while trying to conceive
factors.headline: In the largest preconception cohort, severe depressive symptoms lowered the monthly chance of conceiving (FR 0.62) whether or not they were treated, and psychotropic medication itself did not appear to harm fecundability; a possible miscarriage signal with antidepressants remains unresolved.

dose.effective: Standard therapeutic SSRI doses as prescribed.
dose.studied_range: Self-reported antidepressant use in preconception cohorts (957-2146 women) and infertility-trial cohorts (1650 women).
dose.too_much: No dose threshold established.
dose.timeframe: Associations measured per menstrual cycle over 6-12 months of trying.
dose.notes: Informs, does not prescribe: do not stop, start or change the dose of a prescribed medication without talking to the prescriber. Guidelines (ACOG 2023) support individualized decisions and SSRIs as first-line drug treatment in pregnancy; stopping an effective antidepressant risks relapse, which itself affects fertility and pregnancy.

factors.mechanism: No established oxidative mechanism; serotonin signalling and the hypothalamic-pituitary-ovarian axis may interact, and depression itself affects behaviour, sleep and stress hormones [med-nillni2016].
factors.interactions: [psychological-stress] and [short-sleep] overlap with depression; the male-partner side is covered by [ssri-sperm].
factors.caveats: Confounding by the underlying depression is the central problem in every study.
factors.debate: Reassuring: in PRESTO, medication use did not harm fecundability and depression did [med-nillni2016], and a review found insufficient evidence that SSRIs reduce fertility or IVF outcomes [med-sylvester2019]. Concerning: another cohort found lower cycle-specific fecundability with antidepressants after adjusting for depression history (FR 0.66) [med-casillalennon2016], and maternal antidepressant use was associated with first-trimester loss in infertility trials [med-evanshoeker2018]. ACOG supports continuing effective treatment with shared decision-making [med-acog2023].

factors.name: Hormonal contraception and return of fertility
factors.headline: About 83% of women conceive within 12 months of stopping contraception of any type; injectables delay return of normal fertility by about 5-8 cycles, the patch about 4, the pill or ring about 3, IUDs and implants about 2, and total years of use do not matter.

dose.effective: Not applicable; the question is the delay after stopping.
dose.studied_range: 22 studies of 14,884 women; prospective cohort of 17,954 women trying to conceive.
dose.too_much: Injectable progestin (DMPA) has the longest delay (FR 0.65).
dose.timeframe: Pill, ring: ~3 cycles; patch: ~4; injectable: 5-8; IUD and implant: ~2.
dose.notes: Informs, does not prescribe: do not stop, start or change the dose of a prescribed medication without talking to the prescriber. Plan stopping injectables several months before wanting to conceive. Start folic acid before stopping contraception (see folic-acid).

factors.mechanism: Hormonal methods suppress ovulation; the delay reflects time for the hypothalamic-pituitary-ovarian axis to resume normal cycles, longest with depot injections that persist in the body. No evidence that past use damages eggs.
factors.interactions: Oral contraceptive efficacy is reduced by St John's wort ([supplement-drug-interactions]) and during tirzepatide initiation ([glp1-agonists]). [folic-acid] should begin before stopping.
factors.caveats: Neither study measured egg quality directly; return of fertility is the outcome.
factors.debate: A meta-analysis found no significant delay overall or by method [med-girum2018], whereas a large prospective cohort found short method-specific delays, longest after injectables [med-yland2020]; both agree long-term use does not reduce eventual fertility.

key_numbers.label: Fecundability ratio after injectables vs barrier

factors.name: IVF add-ons (overview)
factors.headline: Most IVF add-ons do not raise live birth: the UK HFEA gives none of 17 rated add-ons a green light for 'having a baby', ESHRE (2023) recommends only hyaluronan transfer medium, and several (PGT-A, endometrial receptivity testing, IVIG, steroids, PRP) carry red ratings for cost, lost embryos or safety.

dose.effective: Default: a standard IVF/ICSI cycle with no paid extras. The only add-on ESHRE recommends is hyaluronan-enriched transfer medium (0.5 mg/mL) combined with single embryo transfer.
dose.studied_range: Add-ons typically cost a few hundred to several thousand GBP/USD per cycle; 82% of Australian IVF patients used at least one.
dose.too_much: Stacking several add-ons multiplies cost and, for invasive ones (PRP, immunotherapy, endometrial biopsy, PGT-A biopsy), risk, without evidence of additive benefit.
dose.timeframe: Per IVF cycle.
dose.notes: Ask the clinic three questions for any extra: what is the HFEA/ESHRE rating, what RCT showed more live births, and what does it cost. Money saved is often better spent on an extra standard cycle.

factors.mechanism: Add-ons target embryo selection (PGT-A, time-lapse), implantation (scratching, embryo glue, hCG, receptivity tests, immune treatments), egg yield or quality (growth hormone, DHEA, PRP, mitochondria, antioxidants) or sperm selection (PICSI, MACS, microfluidics). Most rest on plausible biology or surrogate outcomes (eggs retrieved, embryo grade, pregnancy per transfer) rather than live birth per woman.
factors.interactions: See the individual entries: [endometrial-scratch-egg], [embryo-glue-egg], [assisted-hatching-egg], [time-lapse-egg], [pgt-a-egg], [intrauterine-hcg-egg], [immune-addons-egg], [endometrial-receptivity-egg], [prp-ovarian-egg], [prp-intrauterine-egg], [growth-hormone-ivf-egg], [mitochondrial-augment-egg], [culture-antioxidants-egg], [dhea], [sperm-selection-icsi-sperm], [icsi-non-male-factor-sperm]. Oral antioxidants before IVF are covered in [female-antioxidant-supplements] and [male-antioxidant-combination].
factors.caveats: Absence of evidence is not proof of no effect for a small subgroup, but the burden of proof should sit with the seller. Per-transfer success rates (common in clinic marketing) can rise while live birth per started cycle falls.
factors.debate: Regulators and evidence reviewers (HFEA, ESHRE, Cochrane, Oxford CEBM) conclude that most add-ons lack proof [fer-hfea2026, fer-eshre2023addons, fer-heneghan2016]; ESHRE noted none of its 42 recommendations rested on high-quality evidence. Clinicians and patients often argue that add-ons offer hope where standard care has failed, and surveys show use is widespread and partly patient-driven, though most users later reported regret [fer-lensen2021survey]. Specific add-ons have their own debates (scratching, PGT-A, embryo glue, growth hormone); see their entries.

factors.name: Endometrial scratching before IVF
factors.headline: The 1364-woman PIP trial found identical live birth with and without a scratch (26.1% vs 26.1%); Cochrane 2026 calls the effect unclear (OR 1.12, 0.98-1.28), so at best a small benefit, at the cost of a painful extra procedure.

dose.effective: Not recommended for routine use (ESHRE). Trials used a pipelle biopsy in the luteal phase of the cycle before transfer.
dose.studied_range: One or two pipelle passes, day 3 of the preceding cycle to day 3 of the transfer cycle (PIP).
dose.too_much: Median pain 3.5/10; small infection and bleeding risk.
dose.timeframe: Cycle before embryo transfer.
dose.notes: HFEA amber for most IVF patients, grey for recurrent implantation failure.

factors.mechanism: Hypothesis: controlled injury triggers a local inflammatory and wound-healing response (cytokines, macrophages) that improves endometrial receptivity.
factors.interactions: Often offered alongside [endometrial-receptivity-egg] or [immune-addons-egg] after failed transfers; none has been shown to add up.
factors.caveats: Early small trials were strongly positive; several trials have had data-integrity questions. Benefit, if any, is a few percentage points.
factors.debate: The IPD meta-analysis of 13 integrity-checked RCTs found higher live birth (OR 1.29, 1.02-1.64) [fer-vanhoogenhuijze2023], but its sensitivity analyses crossed 1 and it was publicly criticised [fer-aktoz2024]. The large pragmatic PIP trial was flat [fer-lensen2019] and Cochrane 2026 rates the effect unclear [fer-perera2026]. HFEA rates it amber [fer-hfea2026]; ESHRE does not recommend routine use [fer-eshre2023addons].

factors.name: Hyaluronan-enriched transfer medium ('embryo glue')
factors.headline: The one add-on with a plausible live-birth gain: Cochrane finds about 21% higher live birth (RR 1.21; ~33% to 37-44%) but also 45% more multiple pregnancies, so ESHRE recommends it only with single embryo transfer; HFEA rates it amber.

dose.effective: Hyaluronan 0.5 mg/mL in the transfer medium, with single embryo transfer.
dose.studied_range: 0.5 mg/mL ('functional') vs 0-0.125 mg/mL controls.
dose.too_much: Multiple pregnancy RR 1.45 when more than one embryo is transferred.
dose.timeframe: Embryo is placed in the medium minutes to hours before transfer.
dose.notes: Benefit seen with women's own eggs, not clearly with donor eggs.

factors.mechanism: Hyaluronan is abundant in uterine fluid at implantation; proposed to help embryo-endometrium adhesion via CD44 and to make the medium more viscous.
factors.interactions: Multiple-pregnancy risk interacts with the number of embryos transferred.
factors.caveats: Many trials are older, small and industry-linked; the effect appears in autologous fresh transfers more than frozen ones.
factors.debate: Cochrane (moderate certainty) and a 2022 meta-analysis find a live-birth gain with women's own eggs [fer-heymann2020, fer-heymann2022], and ESHRE recommends it [fer-eshre2023addons]. HFEA judges the evidence conflicting and rates it amber [fer-hfea2026], and in Cochrane's low-risk-of-bias subset the miscarriage benefit disappears [fer-heymann2020].

key_numbers.label: Number needed to treat, own eggs

factors.name: Assisted hatching (laser or chemical zona opening)
factors.headline: Across 14 RCTs reporting live birth, assisted hatching made no clear difference (OR 1.09, 0.92-1.29) and may raise multiple pregnancy (OR 1.38); ESHRE does not recommend it and HFEA rates it grey.

dose.effective: Not recommended.
dose.studied_range: Laser, acid Tyrode's or mechanical thinning/opening of the zona pellucida before transfer.
dose.too_much: Possible embryo damage; more multiple pregnancies and monozygotic twinning.
dose.timeframe: Embryo-transfer day.
dose.notes: Often still used routinely for frozen embryos or older women without trial support.

factors.mechanism: Assumes embryos fail to escape a hardened zona pellucida (e.g. after freezing or with age).
factors.interactions: Trophectoderm biopsy for [pgt-a-egg] already opens the zona.
factors.caveats: Very low to low quality trials with publication bias.
factors.debate: Some clinicians argue for subgroups (frozen embryos, older women, thick zona), but no high-quality subgroup evidence exists [fer-lacey2021]; HFEA and ESHRE do not support it [fer-hfea2026, fer-eshre2023addons].

factors.name: Time-lapse embryo imaging and incubation
factors.headline: Two large double-blind RCTs (TILT, 1575 women; SelecTIMO, 1731 couples) found no live-birth or cumulative-pregnancy gain from time-lapse culture or time-lapse-based selection; HFEA rates it black (no effect).

dose.effective: No benefit for live birth; harmless if the clinic includes it at no extra cost.
dose.studied_range: Time-lapse incubators with manual or algorithmic (e.g. EEVA, KIDScore) embryo selection.
dose.too_much: No known extra risk; cost only.
dose.timeframe: Embryo culture days 0-5.
dose.notes: Useful as a lab-management tool (undisturbed culture, records), not as a success booster.

factors.mechanism: Continuous imaging avoids taking embryos out of the incubator (stable temperature, pH and oxygen, i.e. less culture stress) and adds timing data for selection.
factors.interactions: Often bundled with AI embryo selection; same lack of live-birth data applies.
factors.caveats: Earlier Cochrane evidence was low quality and inconclusive.
factors.debate: Proponents point to the non-significant +3.6 points with undisturbed culture in TILT [fer-bhide2024]; trialists conclude widespread use 'should be questioned' [fer-kieslinger2023]. Cochrane found low-quality, inconclusive evidence [fer-armstrong2019]; HFEA and ESHRE say it does not improve live birth [fer-hfea2026, fer-eshre2023addons].

key_numbers.label: 12-month ongoing pregnancy, time-lapse selection vs standard (SelecTIMO)

factors.name: PGT-A (preimplantation genetic testing for aneuploidy)
factors.headline: PGT-A does not raise live birth per woman and can lower it: in a 1212-woman NEJM trial cumulative live birth was 77.2% with PGT-A vs 81.8% without; it lowers miscarriage per transfer (HFEA green for that) but HFEA rates it red for having a baby, and it roughly doubles IVF cost.

dose.effective: Not recommended routinely (ESHRE, HFEA). Distinct from PGT-M/PGT-SR for known genetic conditions, which are not add-ons.
dose.studied_range: Trophectoderm biopsy of day 5-6 blastocysts with NGS; older trials used day-3 or polar-body biopsy.
dose.too_much: Embryos labelled aneuploid or mosaic may be discarded although some could make healthy babies; some couples end with no transferable embryo.
dose.timeframe: Adds a freeze-all cycle and weeks of delay before transfer.
dose.notes: Per-transfer success looks higher because poor embryos are filtered out before transfer; the fair comparison is live birth per started cycle.

factors.mechanism: Selects embryos without whole-chromosome errors, which rise steeply with maternal age because of cohesin loss in eggs (see [maternal-age]). It cannot create euploid embryos, only choose among those already made, and a 5-10-cell biopsy may misrepresent the embryo (mosaicism).
factors.interactions: Most relevant with advanced [maternal-age]; does not fix egg quality. Combining with [time-lapse-egg] or [assisted-hatching-egg] adds nothing proven.
factors.caveats: Aneuploid calls are very accurate at predicting failure [fer-tiegs2021], which is why the debate is about efficacy per woman, not about test validity.
factors.debate: Supporters cite fewer miscarriages and shorter time to pregnancy in older women (Rubio RCT: miscarriage 2.7% vs 39%, delivery per first transfer 52.9% vs 24.2%) and the STAR post hoc gain at 35-40 [fer-rubio2017, fer-munne2019], plus near-perfect predictive value of aneuploid calls [fer-tiegs2021]. Critics point to unchanged or lower cumulative live birth [fer-yan2021, fer-munne2019, fer-cornelisse2020, fer-iwarsson2026], viable mosaic embryos being discarded (the mosaic study was run by a PGT company) [fer-capalbo2021], and per-transfer reporting that hides losses [fer-paulson2019]. HFEA red for live birth, green for miscarriage [fer-hfea2026]; ESHRE: not for routine use [fer-eshre2023addons].
