factors.name: Intrauterine hCG infusion before embryo transfer
factors.headline: Cochrane found a live-birth benefit only for day-3 (cleavage-stage) transfers with at least 500 IU and no evidence for blastocyst transfer, today's norm; ESHRE does not recommend it.

dose.effective: Not recommended. The only positive subgroup used >=500 IU before cleavage-stage transfer.
dose.studied_range: 100-1000 IU urinary or recombinant hCG infused minutes to days before transfer.
dose.timeframe: Embryo-transfer cycle.
dose.notes: Not on the HFEA rating list.

factors.mechanism: hCG made by the embryo signals to the endometrium (angiogenesis, immune tolerance, decidualisation); infusion aims to mimic this early.
factors.interactions: Irrelevant to most current cycles, which use blastocyst transfer.
factors.caveats: Most trials at high risk of bias, with very high heterogeneity.
factors.debate: Cochrane rated the cleavage-stage >=500 IU benefit as moderate quality [fer-craciunas2018]; ESHRE judged the evidence conflicting and does not recommend it [fer-eshre2023addons].

factors.name: Immunological tests and treatments (IVIG, intralipids, steroids, NK-cell testing)
factors.headline: No good evidence that 'immune' testing or treatment helps IVF: HFEA rates IVIG and steroids red (no proven benefit plus real risks such as thrombosis, infection and preterm birth) and intralipids grey; ESHRE recommends against all of them.

dose.effective: Not recommended outside research or a diagnosed autoimmune disease treated for its own sake.
dose.studied_range: IVIG 0.2-0.5 g/kg infusions; intralipid 20% infusions; prednisolone/dexamethasone around implantation.
dose.too_much: IVIG is a blood product (thrombosis, kidney injury, allergy); steroids raise infection risk, blood pressure and possibly preterm birth; intralipids can cause allergy in soy/egg-allergic people.
dose.timeframe: Given before and after embryo transfer.
dose.notes: Uterine or blood natural-killer-cell tests have no validated link to IVF outcome.

factors.mechanism: Premise that maternal immune cells (especially NK cells) reject the embryo; immune rejection of the fetus 'rarely, if ever, happens' according to HFEA.
factors.interactions: Often sold after recurrent implantation failure; ESHRE's RIF recommendations do not support immunomodulators [fer-eshre2023rif].
factors.caveats: Positive small trials and meta-analyses exist but are low quality.
factors.debate: A meta-analysis mixing RCTs and case-control studies reported higher live birth with IVIG (RR 1.62) [fer-li2013] and a 102-woman RCT reported higher live birth with intralipid (28.8% vs 10%) [fer-singh2019]. Cochrane is uncertain about glucocorticoids (OR 1.37, 0.69-2.71) [fer-boomsma2022]; HFEA (red/grey) and ESHRE reject these treatments [fer-hfea2026, fer-eshre2023addons, fer-eshre2023rif].

factors.name: Endometrial receptivity testing (ERA and similar)
factors.headline: In a 767-patient JAMA trial with euploid embryos, timing transfer by receptivity testing gave no benefit (live birth 58.5% vs 61.9%); HFEA rates it red and ESHRE does not recommend it.

dose.effective: Not recommended.
dose.studied_range: Endometrial biopsy in a mock cycle, gene-expression panel, then 'personalised' transfer timing.
dose.too_much: Extra biopsy (pain, bleeding, rare perforation), a mandatory freeze-all, delay and cost.
dose.timeframe: Adds at least one mock cycle.
dose.notes: Distinct from standard hysteroscopy or treatment of a diagnosed uterine problem.

factors.mechanism: Proposes that some women have a shifted 'window of implantation' detectable by endometrial transcriptomics.
factors.interactions: Often combined with [pgt-a-egg] and [endometrial-scratch-egg] after failed transfers.
factors.caveats: The non-significant direction of the main trial was toward lower live birth.
factors.debate: The test developer's own RCT reported higher per-protocol cumulative live birth (71.2% vs 55.4%) but no intention-to-treat difference and about 50% dropout [fer-simon2020]; the independent JAMA trial was null [fer-doyle2022]. HFEA red [fer-hfea2026]; ESHRE: not recommended [fer-eshre2023addons].

factors.name: Intraovarian platelet-rich plasma ('ovarian rejuvenation')
factors.headline: Two RCTs in poor responders found no gain in euploid embryos (one null on every outcome, one with ~1.5 more mature eggs over three retrievals); HFEA rates it red for safety and lack of evidence, and ESHRE does not recommend it.

dose.effective: Not recommended outside research.
dose.studied_range: Autologous PRP injected transvaginally into each ovary, usually 1-3 months before stimulation.
dose.too_much: Needle injection under anaesthesia: infection, bleeding, anaesthetic risk; no standard preparation.
dose.timeframe: Claims of effect within 1-3 months; not borne out in RCTs.
dose.notes: Marketed for low AMH, perimenopause and premature ovarian insufficiency.

factors.mechanism: Platelet growth factors (PDGF, VEGF, TGF-beta) are claimed to activate dormant follicles or improve the ovarian microenvironment; no human evidence of new or better eggs.
factors.interactions: Does not change [maternal-age]-driven aneuploidy; compare [growth-hormone-ivf-egg] and [dhea] in the same poor-responder population.
factors.caveats: Most supporting studies are uncontrolled case series.
factors.debate: The double-blind Barrenetxea RCT found slightly more cumulative mature eggs (10.45 vs 8.91) but identical euploid blastocysts [fer-barrenetxea2024]; the PROVA RCT found no effect at all [fer-herlihy2024]. Cochrane rates the evidence very low certainty [fer-vaidakis2024]; HFEA red [fer-hfea2026prp]; ESHRE not recommended [fer-eshre2023addons].

key_numbers.label: Mature eggs per cycle, PRP vs control (PROVA)

factors.name: Intrauterine platelet-rich plasma
factors.headline: Pooled small trials suggest higher pregnancy after implantation failure, but the only low-risk-of-bias trial showed no clear effect on live birth (OR 1.10, 0.38-3.14); HFEA rates intrauterine PRP red for every indication.

dose.effective: Not recommended outside research.
dose.studied_range: 0.5-1 mL autologous PRP infused into the uterus 1-2 days before transfer or in the proliferative phase.
dose.too_much: Infection, bleeding, allergic reaction; preparations unstandardised.
dose.timeframe: Embryo-transfer cycle.
dose.notes: Marketed for thin endometrium, recurrent implantation failure and Asherman's syndrome.

factors.mechanism: Growth factors claimed to thicken the endometrium and promote angiogenesis and receptivity.
factors.interactions: Usually offered alongside other implantation add-ons ([endometrial-scratch-egg], [immune-addons-egg]).
factors.caveats: Positive pooled results come from high-risk-of-bias trials.
factors.debate: Including all trials, Cochrane found higher live birth/ongoing pregnancy (OR 2.38) but rated it very low certainty and the low-risk trial was null [fer-vaidakis2024]. HFEA red [fer-hfea2026prp]; ESHRE not recommended [fer-eshre2023addons].

factors.name: Growth hormone for poor responders in IVF
factors.headline: Growth hormone adds about 1.4 eggs in poor responders, and Cochrane pooling suggests more live births (OR 1.77) but at very low certainty; the only placebo-controlled trial focused on live birth (LIGHT) found 14.5% vs 13.7%, and ESHRE does not recommend it.

dose.effective: Not recommended routinely. Trials used about 4-12 IU/day subcutaneously during stimulation.
dose.studied_range: Various regimens, often started in the preceding luteal phase.
dose.too_much: Expensive (often the costliest drug in the cycle); fluid retention, joint pain.
dose.timeframe: During ovarian stimulation.
dose.notes: Not on the HFEA rating list.

factors.mechanism: GH and IGF-1 enhance granulosa-cell FSH sensitivity and steroidogenesis; proposed to improve egg competence and mitochondrial function.
factors.interactions: Same population as [dhea], [coq10] and [prp-ovarian-egg]; none has proven live-birth benefit.
factors.caveats: Small, heterogeneous trials; LIGHT stopped early (113 women), so it was underpowered.
factors.debate: Cochrane pooled 8 small poor-responder trials and found more live births (OR 1.77, 1.17-2.70) but rated it very low certainty [fer-sood2021]; the placebo-controlled LIGHT trial found no difference [fer-norman2019]. ESHRE lists GH among adjuncts not recommended [fer-eshre2023addons].

key_numbers.label: Live birth OR in poor responders (Cochrane, very low certainty)

factors.name: Mitochondrial augmentation (AUGMENT autologous mitochondrial transfer)
factors.headline: The only randomised trial of AUGMENT was discontinued after an interim analysis showed no benefit: fewer blastocysts (23% vs 41%) and the same live birth per transferred embryo (41.6% vs 41.2%), after an extra surgical ovarian biopsy.

dose.effective: Not recommended; ESHRE says mitochondrial replacement to improve egg quality is not recommended.
dose.studied_range: Mitochondria from the woman's own ovarian 'egg precursor' cells, injected with the sperm during ICSI.
dose.too_much: Requires laparoscopic ovarian cortex biopsy; unknown long-term safety for children.
dose.timeframe: One IVF cycle plus a prior biopsy.
dose.notes: Different from mitochondrial donation to prevent mtDNA disease, which is a regulated medical use.

factors.mechanism: Ageing eggs have fewer, less efficient mitochondria (see [maternal-age], [coq10]); adding 'young' mitochondria was meant to restore ATP supply for meiosis and early cleavage.
factors.interactions: Shares its rationale with [coq10] and [nmn-nad]; none has shown live-birth benefit in humans.
factors.caveats: Early positive reports were uncontrolled.
factors.debate: Researchers behind the technique note three early uncontrolled studies (104 patients) suggesting benefit [fer-tilly2020]; the randomised pilot found none and was discontinued [fer-labarta2019]. ESHRE does not recommend mitochondrial replacement for egg quality [fer-eshre2023addons].

factors.name: Antioxidants added to IVF culture media
factors.headline: A single sibling-oocyte RCT (133 patients) found more good day-3 embryos (50% vs 41%) with acetyl-L-carnitine, NAC and alpha-lipoic acid in the medium and higher ongoing pregnancy only in a 35-40 subgroup; no live-birth trial, no HFEA rating.

dose.effective: Unproven; a lab choice, not something patients take.
dose.studied_range: Acetyl-L-carnitine, N-acetyl-L-cysteine and alpha-lipoic acid (A3) at micromolar levels in G-Series media.
dose.timeframe: Fertilisation to blastocyst (days 0-6).
dose.notes: This is the one place an antioxidant acts directly on the embryo in a dish, free of oral bioavailability problems.

factors.mechanism: Embryos in culture are exposed to light, atmospheric handling and metabolic ROS without the oviduct's antioxidant defences; direct scavenging and glutathione support may reduce lipid peroxidation and DNA damage. Low oxygen (5%) culture is the established way to limit this.
factors.interactions: Separate from oral antioxidants, which ESHRE does not recommend ([female-antioxidant-supplements], [male-antioxidant-combination]).
factors.caveats: Industry-developed media; the positive outcomes are surrogates or subgroups.
factors.debate: The trial's developers conclude antioxidants 'may improve' embryo viability [fer-gardner2020]; ESHRE's review of oral antioxidants found no reliable live-birth gain and does not recommend antioxidant therapy in ART, and culture-media supplements remain unendorsed [fer-eshre2023addons]. No independent replication found.

key_numbers.label: Good day-3 embryos, antioxidant vs standard medium

factors.name: Ovarian reserve testing (AMH, antral follicle count)
factors.headline: AMH and antral follicle count predict how many eggs IVF will retrieve (AUC ~0.78 for poor response) but not natural fertility or egg quality: women 30-44 with low AMH conceived as often as those with normal AMH (84% vs 75% by 12 cycles).

dose.effective: Useful before IVF or egg freezing to plan drug dose and expected egg numbers; not a 'fertility test' for women trying naturally.
dose.studied_range: Low AMH commonly <0.7-1.0 ng/mL (5-7 pmol/L); AFC = follicles 2-10 mm on day 2-5 ultrasound.
dose.too_much: Over-interpretation: a low AMH can push people into rushed IVF or costly egg freezing; a normal AMH can falsely reassure.
dose.timeframe: AMH can be drawn any cycle day; falls with hormonal contraception, so retest off it if results drive decisions.
dose.notes: Neither marker adds to age in predicting IVF live birth.

factors.mechanism: AMH is secreted by small growing follicles, so it tracks the number of follicles (quantity), whereas egg quality (euploidy) is driven mainly by age.
factors.interactions: Interpret with [maternal-age]; a young woman with low AMH has fewer but mostly euploid eggs. Relevant to [egg-freezing-egg] planning.
factors.caveats: Assays differ; AMH is high in PCOS and low on the pill.
factors.debate: A pilot cohort found low AMH cut day-specific fecundability (FR 0.38) [fer-steiner2011], but the larger Time to Conceive cohort and EAGeR found no link [fer-steiner2017, fer-zarek2015]; ASRM now says markers poorly predict reproductive potential independent of age [fer-asrm2020reserve]. For menopause, AMH is the best single predictor but too imprecise for individuals [fer-depmann2016, fer-finkelstein2020].

factors.name: Egg freezing (planned / 'social' oocyte cryopreservation)
factors.headline: Egg freezing works best young and in volume: with 10-15 eggs frozen at 35 or under, cumulative live birth reached ~85% vs a ~36% plateau at 36+, but only 9-38% of women ever return to use their eggs, and success after 40 is low.

dose.effective: Freeze at 35 or younger if possible and aim for about 10-15 mature eggs (often 2+ stimulation cycles); at least 8-10 for reasonable success, and expect lower odds per egg when older.
dose.studied_range: Vitrified mature (MII) eggs; mean freezing age in cohorts 36-38.
dose.too_much: Ovarian hyperstimulation, procedure risks and cost of repeated cycles and storage; diminishing returns after 40.
dose.timeframe: One stimulation cycle takes about 2 weeks; eggs keep for years in liquid nitrogen.
dose.notes: Per-egg efficiency is low (about 6% overall per thawed egg) and falls with age at freezing; freezing age, not using age, sets the odds.

factors.mechanism: Vitrification halts egg ageing: aneuploidy risk is fixed at the age of freezing (see [maternal-age]); about 75-85% of eggs survive warming.
factors.interactions: Planning uses [amh-ovarian-reserve-egg] to predict egg yield; later use often involves [pgt-a-egg] (not proven helpful).
factors.caveats: Outcome data come from small numbers of returning users; models (Goldman, Doyle) are partly extrapolated from fresh IVF.
factors.debate: Advocates argue it extends reproductive autonomy and that women should freeze younger [fer-goold2009, fer-cobo2016review]; clinic authors also note it is most cost-effective at 37-38, when biological success is lower [fer-cobo2016review]. Ethicists warn employer-paid schemes may pressure women [fer-mertes2015], and follow-up shows most eggs are never used (38% return at 10-15 years; 15% in Sweden) [fer-blakemore2021, fer-wennberg2019]. ASRM calls it ethically permissible with honest counselling and says live birth cannot yet be predicted precisely [fer-asrm2024ethics, fer-asrm2021oc].

factors.name: Low-dose aspirin to prevent pre-eclampsia
factors.headline: In high-risk pregnancies, aspirin 150 mg nightly from 11-14 weeks cut preterm pre-eclampsia from 4.3% to 1.6% (ASPRE); USPSTF recommends 81 mg/day after 12 weeks for people at high risk.

dose.effective: 81 mg/day after 12 weeks (USPSTF, US) or 150 mg at night from 11-14 weeks to 36 weeks (ASPRE regimen), only when screening shows high risk.
dose.studied_range: 50-150 mg/day in trials.
dose.too_much: May slightly increase postpartum haemorrhage; not for people with aspirin allergy or bleeding disorders.
dose.timeframe: Start before 16 weeks, ideally 12-14; continue to about 36 weeks.
dose.notes: A pregnancy medicine prescribed by the obstetric team, not a preconception supplement; mention prior pre-eclampsia, chronic hypertension, diabetes, kidney or autoimmune disease, IVF and twin pregnancy at booking.

factors.mechanism: Low-dose aspirin irreversibly blocks platelet COX-1 and thromboxane A2 while sparing prostacyclin, improving placental perfusion; it does not act as an antioxidant.
factors.interactions: Contrast with [antioxidants-preeclampsia-egg], which failed despite the oxidative-stress rationale.
factors.caveats: Benefit is for preterm, placenta-driven pre-eclampsia; little effect on term disease. Rated low on the egg-quality scale because it acts in pregnancy (placenta), not on eggs; its effect on preterm pre-eclampsia in high-risk pregnancies is large.
factors.debate: Dose is debated: ASPRE used 150 mg [fer-rolnik2017] while USPSTF recommends 81 mg [fer-uspstf2021]; Cochrane shows a modest 18% reduction across 77 trials (NNT 61) [fer-duley2019]. StopPRE found that stopping at 24-28 weeks in women with normal placental markers was non-inferior [fer-mendoza2023].

factors.name: Vitamin C + E in pregnancy to prevent pre-eclampsia
factors.headline: Four large RCTs (VIP, WHO, US MFMU, DAPIT; about 14,700 women) found vitamin C 1000 mg + E 400 IU did not prevent pre-eclampsia, and pooled data show more low birthweight, gestational hypertension and term rupture of membranes.

dose.effective: None; do not take high-dose C+E for pre-eclampsia.
dose.studied_range: 1000 mg vitamin C + 400 IU vitamin E daily from 9-22 weeks.
dose.too_much: Low birthweight RR 1.15 (VIP); term prelabour rupture of membranes RR 1.77 (Cochrane).
dose.timeframe: From second trimester to delivery in trials.
dose.notes: A standard prenatal vitamin at RDA levels is different and fine.

factors.mechanism: Placental ischaemia-reperfusion and syncytiotrophoblast stress generate oxidative stress in pre-eclampsia, but the disease is driven upstream by defective placentation and antiangiogenic factors that bulk antioxidants do not correct.
factors.interactions: Same failure pattern as [vitamin-c-e-combined] in fertility and cardiovascular trials; [aspirin-preeclampsia-egg] works through a different mechanism.
factors.caveats: A textbook antioxidant paradox: strong biomarker rationale, null hard outcomes.
factors.debate: DAPIT authors suggested women with low antioxidant status might still benefit (pre-eclampsia 15% vs 19%, NS) [fer-mccance2010], and Cochrane found less placental abruption (RR 0.64) [fer-rumbold2015e]. But the large trials were null [fer-poston2006, fer-villar2009, fer-roberts2010], including in low-nutrition populations, and meta-analysis found no benefit with some harms [fer-condeagudelo2011].

factors.name: Iron status and ovulatory fertility
factors.headline: In the Nurses' Health Study II, women taking iron supplements had 40% less ovulatory infertility, but two newer cohorts of 4662 pregnancy planners found no consistent link except in women prone to deficiency; correcting deficiency matters, extra iron does not.

dose.effective: Check ferritin before trying to conceive; if low, treat (see [iron-deficiency]). Prenatal vitamins typically supply 27 mg/day, matching the pregnancy RDA.
dose.studied_range: Dietary and supplemental non-heme iron intakes in cohorts; heme iron showed no association.
dose.too_much: IOM UL 45 mg/day outside treatment; high ferritin in pregnancy is associated with gestational diabetes.
dose.timeframe: Repletion takes about 3 months, similar to the ~3-month follicle development window.
dose.notes: Heavy menstrual bleeding and short cycles are common causes of low iron in women trying to conceive.

factors.mechanism: Iron supports mitochondrial energy production and oxygen delivery to developing follicles. At the other extreme, iron overload in follicular fluid (seen in endometriosis) triggered granulosa-cell ferroptosis and poor oocyte maturation in mouse models, a mechanistic warning against excess.
factors.interactions: Usually delivered via prenatal multivitamins together with folic acid [folic-acid] [multivitamin-mineral]. Endometriosis creates local iron overload [endometriosis].
factors.caveats: Observational and self-reported; women who take supplements differ in many ways. No RCT of iron for fertility in non-anaemic women exists.
factors.debate: Positive: NHS II found iron supplements lowered ovulatory infertility (RR 0.60) [nut-chavarro2006]. Null-to-modest: PRESTO and Snart Foraeldre found no consistent association, with benefit limited to supplement users in North America and women with heavy menses [nut-hahn2019]. Mechanistic data point the other way for local excess [nut-ni2022], and iron-overload disorders cause amenorrhoea [nut-carlomagno2026].

mechanisms.name: ROS as a required ovulation signal
mechanisms.description: A transient burst of reactive oxygen species after the LH surge is needed for cumulus expansion, progesterone production, EGF-receptor/MAPK signalling and follicle rupture. In mice, flooding the ovary with antioxidants reduced ovulation. Oxidative stress is harmful only when ROS are excessive or prolonged, which is one reason high-dose antioxidant supplements are not automatically helpful.

mechanisms.name: Oocyte mitochondria and maternally inherited mtDNA
mechanisms.description: The oocyte is the most mitochondria-rich cell in the body and its mitochondria supply the early embryo until embryonic mitochondrial biogenesis starts. mtDNA is inherited only from the mother (sperm mtDNA is eliminated) and passes through a genetic bottleneck, so oocyte mitochondrial quality matters for the next generation. With age, oocyte mitochondria produce less ATP, mtDNA becomes less stable and CoQ10-synthesis enzymes decline.

mechanisms.name: Cohesin loss and egg aneuploidy
mechanisms.description: Eggs pause in meiosis I from before birth until ovulation. The cohesin complexes that hold chromosome pairs together are not replaced, so they erode over decades; in older women this centromeric cohesion loss drives chromosome mis-segregation, giving a U-shaped aneuploidy curve with a steep rise after the mid-30s. This is the main reason age dominates egg quality, and it is not an oxidative process that antioxidants are known to fix.

mechanisms.name: Declining NAD+ in ageing oocytes
mechanisms.description: In mice, oocyte NAD+ falls with age; restoring it with NMN improved mitochondrial function, spindle assembly and fertility. Human evidence is lacking.

mechanisms.name: Follicular fluid oxidative stress
mechanisms.description: Follicular fluid surrounds the maturing egg. Higher ROS, lipid peroxidation and 8-OHdG (oxidative DNA damage) in follicular fluid are associated with degenerate oocytes, fertilization failure and poor embryos. Obesity raises follicular insulin, triglycerides and CRP. These markers are research tools, not validated clinical tests.

mechanisms.name: Lipotoxicity in obesity
mechanisms.description: Excess lipid in the follicle leads to lipid accumulation in the oocyte, endoplasmic-reticulum stress, loss of mitochondrial membrane potential and cumulus-cell apoptosis, lowering fertilization.

mechanisms.name: The egg repairs sperm DNA damage
mechanisms.description: Until the embryo's own genome switches on (4-8 cell stage), DNA repair relies on maternal transcripts and proteins stored in the egg. Good-quality eggs can partly compensate for sperm DNA fragmentation: in one cohort sperm DNA damage reduced pregnancy with patients' own eggs but not with donor eggs.

mechanisms.name: Folliculogenesis timeline (why 3 months)
mechanisms.description: A resting follicle takes several months to reach the preantral stage, then about 70-85 more days to grow to the selectable 2-5 mm stage and ovulate. The egg ovulated in a given month has therefore been developing in the follicular environment of the preceding ~3 months, which is the window lifestyle changes can influence.

references.authors: Agarwal A, Aponte-Mellado A, Premkumar BJ, et al.
references.title: The effects of oxidative stress on female reproduction: a review
references.finding: Narrative review: oxidative stress is implicated in endometriosis, PCOS, unexplained infertility and pregnancy complications; antioxidant evidence is mostly animal/in-vitro and conflicting.

references.authors: Shkolnik K, Tadmor A, Ben-Dor S, et al.
references.title: Reactive oxygen species are indispensable in ovulation
references.journal: Proc Natl Acad Sci U S A
references.finding: In mice, antioxidants injected into the ovarian bursa reduced ovulation and blocked LH-induced cumulus expansion; H2O2 mimicked LH. ROS are an essential pre-ovulatory signal.

references.authors: May-Panloup P, Boucret L, Chao de la Barca JM, et al.
references.title: Ovarian ageing: the role of mitochondria in oocytes and follicles
references.finding: Oocytes are the most mitochondria-rich cells in the body; ageing-related mtDNA instability and impaired mitochondrial biogenesis in oocytes and granulosa cells are closely linked to declining oocyte quality.

references.authors: Cree LM, Samuels DC, de Sousa Lopes SC, et al.
references.title: A reduction of mitochondrial DNA molecules during embryogenesis explains the rapid segregation of genotypes
references.finding: Mouse study: mtDNA is maternally inherited and passes through a genetic bottleneck (partitioning of mtDNA molecules during embryogenesis and germ-cell proliferation) that explains rapid shifts in heteroplasmy between generations.

references.authors: Franasiak JM, Forman EJ, Hong KH, et al.
references.title: The nature of aneuploidy with increasing age of the female partner: a review of 15,169 consecutive trophectoderm biopsies evaluated with comprehensive chromosomal screening
references.finding: Embryo aneuploidy was lowest at ages 26-30 and rose predictably after 26; the chance of having no euploid embryo was 2-6% at ages 26-37, 33% at 42 and 53% at 44.

references.authors: Gruhn JR, Zielinska AP, Shukla V, et al.
references.title: Chromosome errors in human eggs shape natural fertility over reproductive life span
references.finding: Aneuploidy in human eggs follows a U-curve with age; in older women it is driven by centromeric and more extensive loss of sister-chromatid cohesion.

references.authors: Bertoldo MJ, Listijono DR, Ho WJ, et al.
references.title: NAD(+) Repletion Rescues Female Fertility during Reproductive Aging
references.finding: In aged mice, oocyte NAD+ falls with age; the precursor NMN restored oocyte quality, fertility and embryo development. Mouse data only.

references.authors: Miao Y, Cui Z, Gao Q, et al.
references.title: Nicotinamide Mononucleotide Supplementation Reverses the Declining Quality of Maternally Aged Oocytes
references.finding: In naturally aged mice, NMN restored oocyte NAD+, spindle/chromosome structure, fertilization ability and mitochondrial function and lowered ROS. Mouse data only.

references.authors: Gougeon A
references.title: Dynamics of follicular growth in the human: a model from preliminary results
references.finding: Human follicle growth is very long: the ovulatory follicle comes from a cohort of preantral follicles that differentiated about 85 days earlier; it is recruited 15-20 days before ovulation.

references.authors: Gougeon A
references.title: Human ovarian follicular development: from activation of resting follicles to preovulatory maturation
references.finding: Several months are needed for a growing follicle to reach the preantral stage, then about 70 more days to reach 2 mm before cyclic selection.

references.authors: Das S, Chattopadhyay R, Ghosh S, et al.
references.title: Reactive oxygen species level in follicular fluid--embryo quality marker in IVF?
references.finding: Higher follicular fluid ROS and lipid peroxidation were associated with fertilization failure, pronuclear arrest and poor-grade embryos.

references.authors: Tamura H, Takasaki A, Miwa I, et al.
references.title: Oxidative stress impairs oocyte quality and melatonin protects oocytes from free radical damage and improves fertilization rate
references.finding: Follicular 8-OHdG (oxidative DNA damage) was higher where many oocytes degenerated; melatonin 3 mg/day and/or vitamin E 600 mg/day lowered follicular oxidative markers, and melatonin was associated with better fertilization vs the previous failed cycle (not randomized).

references.authors: Meseguer M, Santiso R, Garrido N, et al.
references.title: Effect of sperm DNA fragmentation on pregnancy outcome depends on oocyte quality
references.finding: Sperm DNA fragmentation lowered pregnancy odds when the woman's own (infertile-patient) oocytes were used, but had no significant effect with donor oocytes, implying good oocytes can compensate for sperm DNA damage.

references.authors: Ménézo Y, Dale B, Cohen M
references.title: DNA damage and repair in human oocytes and embryos: a review
references.finding: Early embryos rely on maternally stored DNA-repair transcripts until embryonic genome activation at the 4-8 cell stage; the oocyte must repair DNA damage brought in by sperm.

references.authors: ACOG Committee on Gynecologic Practice; ASRM Practice Committee
references.title: Female age-related fertility decline. Committee Opinion No. 589
references.finding: ACOG/ASRM: female fecundity declines gradually from about age 32 and more rapidly after 37; evaluate after 6 months of trying at >35 and immediately at >40.

references.authors: Murri M, Luque-Ramírez M, Insenser M, et al.
references.title: Circulating markers of oxidative stress and polycystic ovary syndrome (PCOS): a systematic review and meta-analysis
references.finding: Women with PCOS had higher circulating malondialdehyde (+47%), homocysteine (+23%) and ADMA, and about 50% lower glutathione, independent of weight excess.

references.authors: Teede HJ, Tay CT, Laven JJE, et al.
references.title: Recommendations From the 2023 International Evidence-based Guideline for the Assessment and Management of Polycystic Ovary Syndrome
references.finding: 2023 international PCOS guideline (77 evidence-based, 54 consensus recommendations): emphasizes healthy lifestyle and evidence-based medical and fertility therapy; evidence generally low-to-moderate quality.

references.authors: Sanchez AM, Vanni VS, Bartiromo L, et al.
references.title: Is the oocyte quality affected by endometriosis? A review of the literature
references.finding: Systematic review: oocytes from women with endometriosis are more likely to fail in-vitro maturation, show altered morphology and lower mitochondrial content; granulosa cells show more ROS.

references.authors: Hamdan M, Dunselman G, Li TC, et al.
references.title: The impact of endometrioma on IVF/ICSI outcomes: a systematic review and meta-analysis
references.finding: Endometrioma was associated with fewer oocytes retrieved and more cancelled cycles, but similar live birth rates (OR 0.98); surgery before IVF did not improve outcomes.

references.authors: Wang Q, Ratchford AM, Chi MM, et al.
references.title: Maternal diabetes causes mitochondrial dysfunction and meiotic defects in murine oocytes
references.finding: In diabetic mice, oocytes showed abnormal mitochondrial structure and distribution, lower ATP and TCA metabolites, more spindle defects and higher aneuploidy.

references.authors: Whitworth KW, Baird DD, Stene LC, et al.
references.title: Fecundability among women with type 1 and type 2 diabetes in the Norwegian Mother and Child Cohort Study
references.finding: Fecundability odds were lower in women with type 1 diabetes (FOR 0.76) and type 2 diabetes (FOR 0.64), even with regular cycles.

references.authors: Robker RL, Akison LK, Bennett BD, et al.
references.title: Obese women exhibit differences in ovarian metabolites, hormones, and gene expression compared with moderate-weight women
references.finding: Higher BMI was associated with higher follicular fluid insulin, lactate, triglycerides and C-reactive protein: an altered, more inflammatory follicular environment.

references.authors: Wu LL, Dunning KR, Yang X, et al.
references.title: High-fat diet causes lipotoxicity responses in cumulus-oocyte complexes and decreased fertilization rates
references.finding: High-fat-diet obese mice had lipid-laden oocytes with reduced mitochondrial membrane potential, ER stress, cumulus apoptosis and lower fertilization; ER stress markers were also raised in granulosa cells of obese women.

references.authors: Sermondade N, Huberlant S, Bourhis-Lefebvre V, et al.
references.title: Female obesity is negatively associated with live birth rate following IVF: a systematic review and meta-analysis
references.finding: Obese women (BMI >= 30) had lower live birth rates after IVF than normal-weight women (RR 0.85); worse when combined with PCOS.

references.authors: Kiddy DS, Hamilton-Fairley D, Bush A, et al.
references.title: Improvement in endocrine and ovarian function during dietary treatment of obese women with polycystic ovary syndrome
references.finding: Women who lost more than 5% of body weight on a 1000 kcal diet had lower insulin, higher SHBG and 9 of 11 improved reproductive function; those losing less than 5% did not improve.

references.authors: Mutsaerts MA, van Oers AM, Groen H, et al.
references.title: Randomized Trial of a Lifestyle Program in Obese Infertile Women
references.finding: LIFEstyle trial: a 6-month lifestyle program before fertility treatment (mean loss 4.4 kg) did not increase healthy term singleton births at 24 months (27.1% vs 35.2%; RR 0.77).

references.authors: Einarsson S, Bergh C, Friberg B, et al.
references.title: Weight reduction intervention for obese infertile women prior to IVF: a randomized controlled trial
references.finding: Intensive weight loss (12 weeks 880 kcal/day, mean -9.4 kg) before IVF did not change IVF live birth (29.6% vs 27.5%), but more spontaneous conceptions occurred (10.5% vs 2.6%).

references.authors: Best D, Avenell A, Bhattacharya S
references.title: How effective are weight-loss interventions for improving fertility in women and men who are overweight or obese? A systematic review and meta-analysis of the evidence
references.finding: In overweight/obese women, reduced-calorie diet and exercise interventions increased pregnancy (RR 1.59) and improved ovulation; miscarriage was not reduced.

references.authors: Augood C, Duckitt K, Templeton AA
references.title: Smoking and female infertility: a systematic review and meta-analysis
references.finding: Female smokers had higher odds of infertility (OR 1.60) and lower odds of pregnancy per IVF cycle (OR 0.66).

references.authors: Waylen AL, Metwally M, Jones GL, et al.
references.title: Effects of cigarette smoking upon clinical outcomes of assisted reproduction: a meta-analysis
references.finding: Smokers undergoing ART had lower odds of live birth per cycle (OR 0.54) and clinical pregnancy (OR 0.56) and higher miscarriage (OR 2.65).

references.authors: Zhu D, Chung HF, Pandeya N, et al.
references.title: Relationships between intensity, duration, cumulative dose, and timing of smoking with age at menopause: A pooled analysis of individual data from 17 observational studies
references.finding: Current smokers had about twice the risk of premature (RRR 2.05) and early (1.80) menopause, with clear dose-response; women who had quit more than 10 years earlier had the same risk as never smokers.

references.authors: Freour T, Masson D, Mirallie S, et al.
references.title: Active smoking compromises IVF outcome and affects ovarian reserve
references.finding: Active smokers had lower AMH, fewer mature oocytes (8.6 vs 12.1) and lower clinical pregnancy (10% vs 29.6%) than non-smokers.

references.authors: Practice Committee of the American Society for Reproductive Medicine
references.title: Tobacco or marijuana use and infertility: a committee opinion
references.finding: ASRM committee opinion reviewing deleterious effects of tobacco, nicotine and marijuana on conception, ovarian follicular dynamics, gamete mutations and ART outcomes, and smoking-cessation strategies.

references.authors: Fan D, Liu L, Xia Q, et al.
references.title: Female alcohol consumption and fecundability: a systematic review and dose-response meta-analysis
references.finding: Any alcohol use was associated with lower fecundability (RR 0.87); light (<=12.5 g/day) 0.89, moderate-heavy (>12.5 g/day) 0.77; per 12.5 g/day RR 0.98.

references.authors: Mikkelsen EM, Riis AH, Wise LA, et al.
references.title: Alcohol consumption and fecundability: prospective Danish cohort study
references.finding: Fewer than 14 servings/week had no discernible effect on fecundability; >=14 servings/week FR 0.82 (imprecise).

references.authors: Rossi BV, Berry KF, Hornstein MD, et al.
references.title: Effect of alcohol consumption on in vitro fertilization
references.finding: Women drinking >=4 drinks/week had 16% lower odds of IVF live birth (OR 0.84); 21% lower when both partners did.

references.authors: Abadia L, Chiu YH, Williams PL, et al.
references.title: The association between pre-treatment maternal alcohol and caffeine intake and outcomes of assisted reproduction in a prospectively followed cohort
references.finding: Low-to-moderate pre-treatment alcohol (<=12 g/day) and caffeine (<200 mg/day) were not associated with ART outcomes.

references.authors: Lyngsø J, Ramlau-Hansen CH, Bay B, et al.
references.title: Association between coffee or caffeine consumption and fecundity and fertility: a systematic review and dose-response meta-analysis
references.finding: Caffeine was associated with spontaneous abortion (RR 1.37 at 300 mg/day; 2.32 at 600 mg/day) but showed little or no association with fecundability or fertility-treatment outcomes.

references.authors: Wesselink AK, Wise LA, Rothman KJ, et al.
references.title: Caffeine and caffeinated beverage consumption and fecundability in a preconception cohort
references.finding: Female total caffeine intake was not associated with fecundability; male intake >=300 mg/day was (FR 0.72).

references.authors: Chen LW, Wu Y, Neelakantan N, et al.
references.title: Maternal caffeine intake during pregnancy and risk of pregnancy loss: a categorical and dose-response meta-analysis of prospective studies
references.finding: Caffeine in pregnancy: pregnancy-loss RR 1.02 at 50-149 mg/day, 1.16 at 150-349, 1.40 at 350-699, 1.72 at >=700; +7% per 100 mg/day.

references.authors: ASRM Practice Committee and SREI Practice Committee
references.title: Optimizing natural fertility: a committee opinion
references.finding: ASRM/SREI: >500 mg caffeine/day linked to lower fertility, 1-2 cups/day has no apparent effect; >2 drinks/day best avoided; folic acid >=400 ug/day; insufficient evidence that a specific diet improves natural fertility.

references.authors: Legro RS, Sauer MV, Mottla GL, et al.
references.title: Effect of air quality on assisted human reproduction
references.finding: Higher NO2 at home and at the IVF lab was associated with lower live birth (e.g. OR 0.76 per 0.01 ppm after embryo transfer); PM2.5 during culture was associated with lower conception.

references.authors: La Marca A, Spaggiari G, Domenici D, et al.
references.title: Elevated levels of nitrous dioxide are associated with lower AMH levels: a real-world analysis
references.finding: Higher NO2 (and weakly PM10/PM2.5) exposure was associated with lower AMH; NO2 remained associated after age adjustment.

references.authors: Gaskins AJ, Mínguez-Alarcón L, Fong KC, et al.
references.title: Supplemental Folate and the Relationship Between Traffic-Related Air Pollution and Livebirth Among Women Undergoing Assisted Reproduction
references.finding: Among women taking <800 ug/day supplemental folate, each 20 ppb NO2 was associated with 24% lower odds of live birth; no association at >=800 ug/day.

references.authors: Hauser R, Gaskins AJ, Souter I, et al.
references.title: Urinary Phthalate Metabolite Concentrations and Reproductive Outcomes among Women Undergoing in Vitro Fertilization: Results from the EARTH Study
references.finding: Highest vs lowest quartile of urinary DEHP metabolites: fewer oocytes and mature oocytes, and 19 percentage points lower clinical pregnancy and live birth per cycle.

references.authors: Mok-Lin E, Ehrlich S, Williams PL, et al.
references.title: Urinary bisphenol A concentrations and ovarian response among women undergoing IVF
references.finding: Each log-unit increase in urinary BPA was associated with 12% fewer oocytes retrieved and lower peak estradiol.

references.authors: Butts CD, Bloom MS, McGough A, et al.
references.title: Toxic elements in follicular fluid adversely influence the likelihood of pregnancy and live birth in women undergoing IVF
references.finding: Follicular fluid mercury above ~0.51 ug/L and higher lead were associated with lower live birth after IVF (Pb RR 0.68).

references.authors: Wallace WH, Thomson AB, Kelsey TW
references.title: The radiosensitivity of the human oocyte
references.finding: Modelling estimates the radiation dose that destroys half of human oocytes (LD50) at less than 2 Gy.

references.authors: Oktay K, Harvey BE, Partridge AH, et al.
references.title: Fertility Preservation in Patients With Cancer: ASCO Clinical Practice Guideline Update
references.finding: ASCO: discuss infertility risk before cancer treatment as early as possible; oocyte and embryo cryopreservation are standard; GnRH agonists are not a substitute for proven preservation methods.

references.authors: Mountjoy M, Ackerman KE, Bailey DM, et al.
references.title: 2023 International Olympic Committee's (IOC) consensus statement on Relative Energy Deficiency in Sport (REDs)
references.finding: IOC 2023 consensus on Relative Energy Deficiency in Sport: low energy availability causes health effects including reproductive dysfunction, with a clinical assessment tool for diagnosis.

references.authors: Gudmundsdottir SL, Flanders WD, Augestad LB
references.title: Physical activity and fertility in women: the North-Trøndelag Health Study
references.finding: Women active on most days had 3.2-fold odds of fertility problems and exercising to exhaustion 2.3-fold, vs low activity; no association at lower activity levels.

references.authors: Wise LA, Rothman KJ, Mikkelsen EM, et al.
references.title: A prospective cohort study of physical activity and time to pregnancy
references.finding: Vigorous activity >=5 h/week vs none: fecundability ratio 0.68 (lean women); moderate activity >=5 h/week: 1.18; no harm from vigorous activity in women with BMI >=25.

references.title: Maternal physical and sedentary activities in relation to reproductive outcomes following IVF
references.finding: Pre-treatment moderate-to-vigorous activity (median 2.8 h/week) was not associated with IVF outcomes; some vigorous activities were associated with higher live birth.

references.authors: Mena GP, Mielke GI, Brown WJ
references.title: The effect of physical activity on reproductive health outcomes in young women: a systematic review and meta-analysis
references.finding: Physical-activity interventions increased pregnancy (RR 2.10) and live birth (RR 2.11) vs no therapy in women with reproductive problems (small number of trials).

references.authors: Stocker LJ, Macklon NS, Cheong YC, et al.
references.title: Influence of shift work on early reproductive outcomes: a systematic review and meta-analysis
references.finding: Shift work was associated with menstrual disruption (aOR 1.15); infertility association was not robust after adjustment (aOR 1.11); night shifts were associated with early pregnancy loss (aOR 1.41).

references.title: Female sleep patterns, shift work, and fecundability in a North American preconception cohort study
references.finding: Trouble sleeping >50% of the time was associated with lower fecundability (FR 0.87); <6 h sleep FR 0.89 (imprecise); shift work was not associated.

references.authors: Lynch CD, Sundaram R, Maisog JM, et al.
references.title: Preconception stress increases the risk of infertility: results from a couple-based prospective cohort study--the LIFE study
references.finding: Highest vs lowest tertile of salivary alpha-amylase (stress marker) was associated with 29% lower fecundability and 2-fold infertility risk; cortisol was not associated.

references.authors: Boivin J, Griffiths E, Venetis CA
references.title: Emotional distress in infertile women and failure of assisted reproductive technologies: meta-analysis of prospective psychosocial studies
references.finding: Pre-treatment anxiety or depression was not associated with pregnancy after a cycle of ART.

references.title: Adherence to the Mediterranean diet and IVF success rate among non-obese women attempting fertility
references.finding: Lowest vs highest tertile of Mediterranean diet score had lower live birth (26.6% vs 48.8%; adjusted RR 0.32); association seen only in women under 35; no effect on oocyte or embryo measures.

references.authors: Gaskins AJ, Nassan FL, Chiu YH, et al.
references.title: Dietary patterns and outcomes of assisted reproduction
references.finding: The profertility diet was associated with 53% higher odds of live birth per SD; top vs bottom quartile +28 percentage points; not related to oocyte counts. Mediterranean diet benefit plateaued after the second quartile.
